There are four characters on screen, and they all move in semi-random patterns. The impostor has to move like an NPC and go unnoticed. If the shooter hits the impostor, the shooter wins. Otherwise, if the shooter hits an innocent bystander, the impostor wins.
That’s all. Each round is a brief game of cat-and-mouse. There is no score, no ultimate goal, no story. One player has to move like an NPC; the other has to shoot the character who moves most suspiciously. That’s all!
It’s a great party game. Grab a bunch of people and take turns playing the shooter and the impostor. This game was a big hit when I gave it to a bunch of kids during a birthday party. They were having lots of fun figuring out how the Zapper works, how the NPCs move, how to outsmart each other. If you ever want to liven up a gathering, try playing this game for a little while!

articles.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.
Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.
China
China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday, a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.
Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.
Singapore
In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.
In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.
South Korea
South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.
Taiwan
Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media. Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.
Japan
In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

articles.title: A short history of the honey trap
articles.body:
A short history of the honey trap
- November 12, 2026
- Marc Polymeropoulos
Sex and espionage – two of the world’s oldest professions – have long collided.
We have ourselves a good old fashioned spy scandal. Tabloids around the world are filled with salacious stories, with headlines such as the never-to-disappoint New York Post’s ‘Huang For Her Buck’ and ‘Huang Huang Bang Bang’ running this week. Readers have been transfixed, as two of the oldest professions – sex and espionage – collide.
The practitioners of espionage – the second oldest profession – always seek to take advantage of a target’s vulnerabilities. An intelligence service seeks to recruit targets based on the ‘MICE’ principle, which includes Money, Ideology, Coercion and Ego as key motivating factors.
So let’s go back to the basic concept of the honey trap. And the history of such honey traps is rich indeed. Mata Hari, a Dutch exotic dancer who was convicted of spying for Germany during the First World War and accused of seducing the French elite, always comes to mind, as her name is synonymous with such techniques. And the famous East German spymaster Markus Wolf used male ‘Romeos’ to entrap West German secretaries during the Cold War. Honey traps are not solely carried out by female ‘sparrows’, but by males as well. The CIA website in fact has many accounts of such cases from the notorious East German Stasi. ‘Felix’ was one of the first ‘Romeos’, who moved to West Germany in the 1950s, and recruited ‘Norma’, a West German government employee, who passed him secrets from the West German chancellery. According to the CIA, 40 women were prosecuted in West Germany during the Cold War for espionage.
The history of honey traps has all sorts of different flavours. The Soviet KGB in the 1950s recruited John Vassall, an employee at the British embassy in Moscow, photographing him in compromising circumstances with men – by later accounts, after drugging him. They threatened him with exposure, and he ended up passing a great many documents to the KGB. And in the 1980s, a US Marine Security Guard at the embassy in Moscow, Clayton Lonetree, fell for a KGB honey trap. He was recruited by the Soviets and passed sensitive information to the KGB.
Do all honey traps work on all targets? Well, not really. Culture matters. The French are a perfect example. In the French documentary ‘The Making of Secret Agents’, a French intelligence officer known as Nicolas states that the paradox for many French is that extramarital affairs are so commonplace that they provide a hostile service little if any leverage. It is slightly amusing that the threat of telling one’s spouse would result in a simple shrug. The French being the French, maybe other elements of MICE are more appropriate for them.
Here’s a small nugget for intelligence aficionados to chew on: as per opensource reporting, US intelligence is not fond of utilising such honey-trap tactics. No, it’s not because my old colleagues were ‘too woke’ to stoop to such unsavoury measures, a charge I saw recently bandied about on social media. Instead, there reportedly are practical reasons for this. Blackmail doesn’t make for productive long-term agents, many former case officers say. It is far preferable to gain an agent’s trust if they believe they are doing it for the right reasons, for example. Think back to the ‘MICE’ principle. An agent who hated communism, or an agent who needed money for one of his children’s medical bills, is always going to be more productive, more trustworthy, and more likely to remain in place for an extended period of time, rather than someone who is being blackmailed because of sexual proclivities.
Finally, every piece like this needs not just historical context, but a personal story. In the 1990s I was sent to the Balkans on behalf of the US government to help a friendly government in the counter-terrorism arena. This country had a communist past, and thus there were likely several holdovers from the old pro-Soviet era in their intelligence services. Well, leaving my hotel room one day, I walked down the hallway of a five-storey hotel, and lo and behold a door opened to the side of me. In the dead of winter, two young ladies in bikinis asked me by name to come into their room and ‘fix their broken minibar’. I laughed and, while I was impressed by their moxie to take a run at me, their crooked teeth (and my counterintelligence training) gave me enough of a pause to keep on walking. Later on, playing pool with a very senior member of that intelligence service which had just taken a shot at me, I asked what the hell had just happened. My counterpart smiled and said: ‘it’s the old guard, what can we do?’ as he calmly sank the eight ball in the side pocket.

articles.title: Lutnick Pushed to Weaken Chip Rules That Overlap with His Family Business
articles.body:
Supported by
Lutnick Pushed to Weaken Chip Rules That Overlap With His Family Business
The commerce secretary has been writing new rules that would affect Southeast Asian data centers, some of which are clients of his former firm.
In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.
The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.
The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.
Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms.
The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.
Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

articles.title: Was America's Nationwide Grounding of Aircraft Caused By Its New AI System?
articles.body:
America Cancels 4,000 More Flights. FAA Denies Impact of New AI System. (kxan.com) 65
			
		 	
				UPDATE:  FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that U,S. airlines will likely cancel 4,000 to 5,000 of the roughly 41,000 flights scheduled for Saturday, reports Yahoo News. And as to the cause of the incident...
[U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean] Duffy said a router involved in the switch from copper wire to fiber "started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system." The system saw "over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds," he said. That disrupted communications with airplanes and radar. 
America's nationwide grounding of flights on Friday happened "amid growing scrutiny... of a new AI-powered air traffic management system" deployed by America's Federal Aviation Administration, reports Texas news station KXAN.  
Ironically, that system is called SMART — but the outage happened "following warnings" from members of the U.S. Congress about this new AI system's safety, reliability and oversight:
In an Oct. 13 letter to the Government Accountability Office, more than 20 members of Congress requested an independent review of the FAA's development and implementation of its Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART. The lawmakers questioned whether the technology was being deployed with adequate input from frontline air traffic controllers, sufficient training and appropriate safety evaluations...  In their letter to the GAO, the lawmakers specifically questioned whether the FAA had adequately evaluated risks associated with SMART's artificial intelligence capabilities, including the potential for the technology to interfere with experienced controllers' decision-making or generate inaccurate safety-critical information.  "The nation's frontline aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART's development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process," the lawmakers wrote. The letter also questioned the FAA's decision to initially pilot the technology in heavily congested airspace, including the National Capital Region.  
"Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data," U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged Friday.
But FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that officials have found "zero evidence of anything AI related" in Friday's outage, according to Yahoo News.
An article from The Hill.com notes that Duffy also said the new AI tool had nothing to do with the ground stop, and that he said the system "isn't plugged in."
"This is completely disconnected, and I love that some people have said this would be the root cause. By the way, if it was, I'll tell you that, but this is not even plugged in," he said. "So, there's no possible way SMART would have impacted."
Duffy also asked Congress for $50 billion to rebuild what he described as an "incredibly old" air traffic control system.
 
Duffy had posted the day before that the AI system had been at least partially rolled out and that it was already working (adding "Soon this technology is going NATIONWIDE")
And Friday CNN's aviation analyst said they believed that AI system could be connected to the nationwide outage, calling it "a tremendous amount of coincidence," according to a report from Mediaite:
 CNN Aviation Analyst: "Many times in the past, what we have seen, and this has gone back decades, is that because air traffic control is this piecemeal, mishmash of a whole bunch of different systems...  some going back to radio, telephones and floppy disks... when they put in new computer systems, they often have difficulty talking with, communicating with, or working with the much older systems. And I have to say, it's a tremendous amount of coincidence...  If they're putting in new software now, this new SMART system to start managing that, and now we have a communications outage, I'm — we've seen this so many times in the past. I don't know if they're linked, but it's just too much coincidence that they were trying to start that moving today, and now we have problems with the en route system.
So if I was to guess — and we haven't heard any, you know, it's not that it's threats or criminals or terrorists. We haven't heard anything like that. So I am guessing that once again we have a problem with new air traffic control computer systems, AI — you know, modern systems trying to communicate with old systems.  And we have just seen this so many times in the past, and it's a big problem... Our whole national airspace system is you know, pieces and parts. It's kind of a Franken-system.  And that would be my guess, that they are having computer issues by putting the new software in with the old, just because today they announced that that were going to do this new system. 
KXAN describes some of the complexity of the newly-launched AI system:
According to the FAA, the system consolidates approximately 200 data streams, including airline schedules, flight paths, weather patterns, airport capacity, airspace conditions and air traffic controller staffing metrics. The agency says SMART uses artificial intelligence to analyze that information, predict traffic flows, identify potential conflicts and recommend adjustments to flight routes and departure schedules before disruptions occur. The FAA describes the technology as a shift from a reactive approach to a predictive one, allowing aviation officials to identify congestion, weather-related restrictions and other operational problems hours, days or even weeks in advance...
The congressional letter raised questions about whether the FAA's implementation strategy was moving faster than its safety evaluations, workforce training and independent oversight could support.
 
Ironically, the article points out that the FAA promoted anticipated benefits from the technology including fewer delays and flight cancellations.  (Other anticipated benefits included improved on-time performance and faster recovery from weather disruptions.)  Although the FAA has realized one of the system's anticipated benefits:  reduced fuel consumption.

articles.title: The Telephone Changed the World
articles.body:
How the Telephone Changed the World
James Gleick Explores the Technological and Cultural Impact of an Invention That Transformed Civilization
A beige plastic telephone sits on a wooden table. The handset, attached by a coiled cord, rests in its cradle. The base has a clear dial with ten finger holes. The telephone is the most ordinary of household objects but, sitting silently on the table, it seems to portend something. It’s bound to ring.
Suddenly it does: a metallic brrrrring, distinctive and familiar. Nearby on the carpet, a smiling girl with pigtails and a ruffled-sleeve dress leaps to her feet, races over, and picks up the handset. She holds a stuffed toy duck to the receiver. Quack! Quack! Quack!
“That’s no way to answer the phone, Susie!” says an older boy, appearing in the frame. He has neatly brushed brown hair and wears a white shirt buttoned to the neck. He grabs the handset from Susie and demonstrates proper etiquette: “Hello. Matthews residence. This is Jimmy.” He listens and speaks again. “Just a minute, please.”
A grown-up arrives, smiling, also wearing his hair neatly parted, with a button-down shirt and khaki trousers. “Uncle Bill,” Jimmy tells him earnestly, “Captain Adams wants to talk to you.”
“Thanks, Jimmy,” says Bill. He takes the handset and holds it to his ear, stretching its coiled cord. “Hi, Captain, this is Bill,” he says. “No, we don’t usually have ducks answer the phone. That one belongs to Susie.” No time for jokes, though. Captain Adams needs Uncle Bill to come at once. These are the whitest white people you’ve ever seen, performing a fantasy of middle-class American life familiar from TV sitcoms that featured Wally and Beaver, Mike and Robbie and Chip.
Eighty-nine years into the telephone era, this wholesome scene opened a movie called We Learn About the Telephone, made in Technicolor on behalf of American Telephone and Telegraph (AT&T) by a well-known Hollywood producer, Jerry Fairbanks. The film was distributed as a public service to schools around the country and played for a captive audience of children in classrooms. In 1965, the United States had one telephone for every four people; the number had tripled in the two decades since World War II. It already seemed the universal appliance. Yet the phone company—there was basically just one—still thought its customers needed instruction.
Back to the show. Little Jimmy asks: “What did people do before the telephone was invented? How’d they get messages to each other in a hurry?”
The paradox of the telephone was its plainness, its tendency to hide in the background while changing everything around it.
Thus prompted, Uncle Bill draws a cartoon character called Mister Man, who begins to speak. (If his voice sounds familiar, it’s because AT&T hired the best: Mel Blanc, the onetime vaudevillian who voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, and many other characters.) Mister Man guides us through a potted history of human communication, beginning with the “cave men” and the Egyptians. “The only way Mr. Caveman knew how to get a message from one place to another was to send a runner,” Bill explains. Greeks used runners, too, and Romans, until they discovered horses. Then came knights and cowboys. “That’s a Pony Express rider!” says Jimmy. “That’s right,” Bill replies. “But man wanted to send messages faster than a runner or a horse could travel.” A cartoon Indian sends smoke signals. Sailors communicate from ship to ship with flashing mirrors and blinking lights. Then the telegraph appears. “Man has always been able to solve his problems by inventing new things…The telegraph was, and still is, wonderful,” Uncle Bill explains. But the telegraph was not enough. “Mister Man wanted to send his voice over a distance, to carry on a real conversation,” Uncle Bill continues. “Then in 1876 a man named Alexander Graham Bell found a way. He invented the telephone.”
This was the story in a nutshell. It was not entirely true, but it served as the essential origin story of its sponsor, the greatest commercial enterprise the world had ever known. AT&T, known as the Bell System, held more capital and generated more income than most nation-states. Its scientific research arm, the Bell Telephone Laboratories, was unique in the world, eventually the source of eleven Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry. Mister Man was right to place the telephone at the head of a line of increasingly powerful information technologies. Humanity had learned to send its voice—its many voices—disembodied, far and wide, eliminating walls, bridging towns and countryside, inviting conversation with strangers unseen.
No single genius accomplished that, and it didn’t happen all at once. No one had felt the absence of telephones before they existed, and at first hardly anyone understood what they might be good for. Much that seems obvious in retrospect had to be learned by people feeling their way toward the future.
*
AT&T had no trouble inserting its potted history into the curriculum of millions of primary-school children, and after the history lesson came some instruction in how to use the device. It was hardly necessary. Most people had a telephone at home that looked exactly like the one in the movie. The Western Electric model 500 was ubiquitous across the United States. It first appeared in 1949 and hardly changed as the years passed: a thermoplastic shell screwed to a metal base, a clear plastic finger wheel, and a handset with a mouthpiece and an ear-piece attached by a cord twisted in a stiff spiral. The phone was heavy, about four pounds, but a person could pick it up with two fingers under the cradle while nestling the handset between shoulder and neck. That was actually comfortable, when people got used to it. If they opened the base by turning it over and removing some screws, they could see a pair of brass bells, with a small clapper between them, and a few colored wires. Ordinary as it was, it spoke of modernity, with its sculpted plastic. No other household gadget had anything like that dial.
When the telephone rang, it did not chirp or chime or play a tune; it just rang. The sound was the same throughout the United States and much of the world: an electromechanical bell ringing for two seconds at a time, with a four-second pause in between. (Older people will never forget that sound, and it can still be heard in old movies and television shows. Nostalgists have been known to install “Old Telephone” as the ringtone for their smartphone.)
At first the telephones were all black; then AT&T customers could choose among ivory, gray, beige, and a few more colors. The phones remained simple, undramatic, and unadorned. Yet they ripped invisible tunnels through space—like wormholes, only real.
More than eight in ten homes in the United States had a Bell System telephone—owned by the company, merely on loan to the customer. No other company was allowed to manufacture telephones, and everyone’s telephones were the same. People thought that was a normal state of affairs: it had always been like that and it always would be.
The phone was a simple object with not so much as an on-off switch, but the Bell System never stopped educating the public in its proper use. Uncle Bill and Mister Man offered children some dos and don’ts. Don’t shout into the telephone. Do use your normal speaking voice. Speak directly into the mouthpiece. It’s important to speak clearly. Don’t let the phone ring too long before answering—“but if you’re the person making the call, you should let the phone ring eight to ten times.”
There is even a lesson in dialing, using the finger wheel to choose the desired telephone number: “When you dial, you should make sure you bring your finger all the way around to the finger stop. Then for each number let the dial go all the way back by itself. Each number. All the way. Then let go. See?”
Everyone knew how to dial the phone. It was no harder than, for example, learning to tie one’s shoelaces. But the Bell System left little to chance. It was relentless. Far more than outsiders knew, it had made itself the author of its own story. The company subsidized books by supposedly independent authors; it sponsored articles, speeches, and pamphlets; and it arranged lectures for business schools and law schools on such matters as public-utility regulation. The slick Jerry Fairbanks movie was one of many instructional films and cartoons. Schoolteachers received a twenty-four-page booklet, also titled We Learn About the Telephone, full of helpful material. A section called “The Telephone Brings Everybody Together” listed, with illustrations, some of the people you can call: the repairman, storekeepers, the fireman, the policeman, and the doctor.
Half a century earlier, the Bell System advertised itself as “The Sign Board of Civilization.” Its full name was the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and Associated Companies. Its logo was a great bell, deliberately resembling the Liberty Bell, bearing the words “Local and Long Distance Telephone.” Advertisements in magazines and newspapers said:
Wherever you see this sign, it stands for civilization. It is the sign of one of the most powerful influences for broadening human intelligence…
Bell telephone service has brought the entire country up to the same instant of progress.
It has unified the Nation…
You can see this march of progress right in your own neighborhood. Every little while some neighbor has a Bell telephone put in. If you have one, every new subscriber enlarges the scope of your personal contact.
The copywriters could not resist adding a threat: “If you have not, every new telephone makes you the more isolated.” This was the essence of the company’s business model: every new subscriber adds value for every other.
*
Children in 1965 were growing up in a world transformed, normal though it seemed to them. Everyone had from birth at least a vague awareness of an invisible web of voices, bringing the unreachable within reach. It was already hard to remember the earlier world, where the loudest shout would barely carry to the next room. The paradox of the telephone was its plainness, its tendency to hide in the background while changing everything around it. When the telephone was still new, Marcel Proust in France saw it already growing old and familiar, “a supernatural instrument before whose miracles we used to stand amazed, and which we now employ without giving it a thought, to summon our tailor or order an ice cream.”
By 1965, teaching children how to dial the telephone was unnecessary. But in the next century the knowledge would be lost again, and YouTube would feature videos of youngsters baffled by ancient rotary telephones. “This is like phones that my mom used as a kid?” “How does this even work?” “It looks like a phone, it has a telephone and it has numbers.”
The telephone had other inventors besides Alexander Graham Bell, an amateur who did not know much about electricity. Neither the idea nor the device came to any one person in a visionary flash. Even with the new invention in hand, the most expert entrepreneurs and government officials had trouble seeing what it was for. The president of the Western Union Telegraph Company dismissed it. “What use could this company make of an electrical toy?” he said, thus condemning his business to stagnation and decline. We might say the telephone was invented by the people who used it. They made it what it is, creating new habits and a new language as they went. Or we might say the telephone invented itself: it was an inevitability; it had to come, and when it came it could not be stopped, an invasive species dragging its wires through cracks in the familiar world.
We have learned by now that gadgets can have a life of their own and an influence we cannot evade. Using a technology changes a person. Using a technology changes a culture.
First the telephone was a curiosity, then a luxury item, and then an ordinary necessity. In 1965, people made something like 100 billion telephone calls a year, long and short, local and long-distance; that number has increased a thousand-fold, but even then the telephone had helped humanity coalesce into a wired collective—trading news and rumors, mingling public intelligence with private gossip. The telephone company could help its customers learn about the telephone, but it could hardly explain the changes that four-pound box of plastic and metal had already worked in the fabric of modern life and in the psyches of the people who put their ears and mouths to it.
The telephone enabled the expansion of cities and the creation of suburbs by freeing workspaces and living spaces from the requirement of proximity. It encouraged nationhood by softening the differences between regions. “The service of the telephone in the consolidation of our Union was an epoch-making service,” wrote Michael Pupin at Columbia University in 1930. “No other country availed itself of the consolidating power of the telephone as much as this country did. No other country needed it so much.”
The telephone brought a generation of women into the workforce for the first time. The job of telephone operator—a profession like none that had ever existed—required intelligence, physical dexterity, mental focus, and genial patience, and it was decided by universal consent that the job belonged to women.
The telephone marked the beginning of a rebalancing of the senses in human culture: it re-centered sound and hearing, which had been deprecated during the long rise of text as the mode of communication most reliable, most stable, most respected. “As there was an Enlightenment, so too was there an ‘Ensoniment,’” argues Jonathan Sterne, a scholar of media and culture. That rebalancing continues.
Was it a connector, a unifier? Or a disrupter of precious solitude? Sociologists argued about what the telephone had done to shape the evolution of modern culture, to alter social habits and relationships. They even argued about whether it could have done anything—whether any technology in itself could dictate human affairs. Some doubted that. People made the telephone, some said; people decided how to use it, so let’s not fall into the trap of granting it agency. The violin doesn’t play the violinist. “No single invention—and no group of them taken together in isolation from nontechnological elements—ever changed the direction in which a society was going,” George Daniels wrote in 1970. “Habits seem to grow out of other habits far more directly than they do out of gadgets.”
But we have learned by now that gadgets can have a life of their own and an influence we cannot evade. Using a technology changes a person. Using a technology changes a culture.
After the telegraph laid the groundwork, establishing the possibility of nearly instantaneous long-distance communication across networks of wires, the telephone became the first piece of what later coalesced into the phenomenon called mass media—the incessant, ubiquitous exchange of information conducted point-to-point via telephones and telefaxes, broadcast via radio and television, and stored and shared as phonographs, photographs, and cinema. Media, distinct from mechanism, required theorists, such as Marshall McLuhan, who asserted its primacy with his clever slogan “The medium is the message.”
The telephone became a cultural artifact and a generator of other artifacts. The ability to speak across space transformed business organizations, military tactics, the rules of etiquette, the rituals of romance. Each profession evolved in its own way, from news gathering to sex work. (“The prostitute was a specialist, and the call-girl is not,” McLuhan declared coolly in 1965.) Other powerful technologies arose alongside the telephone and followed after, but the telephone was special. It conferred upon every individual a power to communicate that was essential in the development of modern life.
It left a trail of appurtenances: the party line, the busy signal, the dial tone, the collect call, the wiretap, the answering machine, the telephone book, the telephone booth. Telephone booths, boxes, kiosks, and cabins, varying from country to country, appeared on public sidewalks; these structures had no other purpose but to house telephones and shelter their users. Anyone old enough to remember telephone booths retains a mental image of a characteristic design—in Britain, a cast-iron box, usually painted red, with a rounded roof, a single door, two mullioned windows, and a classical pediment bearing the royal crest. Some urban children imagined that pay phones whisked their coins through underground pipes to a central repository. Besides allowing people to make calls in semi-privacy, telephone booths spun off oddities of their own. In the mid-twentieth century, pranksters competed to see how many people could squeeze into a telephone booth at once. The comic-book hero Superman used telephone booths to shed his civilian garb; this became so familiar a trope that it inspired a sight gag in the 1978 movie Superman in which Clark Kent dashed for a phone booth and was dismayed to find its modern replacement, a pay phone mounted on a post. Special heroes required special phones: Dick Tracy a wrist radio, Batman his Bat Phone, and Maxwell Smart his shoe phone. Star Trek’s spacefarers had flip phones (“communicators”) twenty years before such things appeared in real life. Meanwhile, the science-fiction paladin Doctor Who traveled through space and time in a vehicle that took the form of the British telephone box. It was bigger on the inside than it appeared from the outside. All phone booths were.
And then, in an eye blink, the phone booths were left to rust, the phone books stopped arriving at the door, and the busy signal and the party line and all the rest became memories. The telephone turned into something else entirely.
______________________________
From The Telephone: A New History by James Gleick. Copyright © 2026. Published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux, a division of Macmillan.
James Gleick
James Gleick is a historian and biographer whose books include The Information, winner of the Royal Society and PEN/America science-writing prizes, and Chaos, a Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award finalist. They have been translated into thirty languages. He lives in New York and London.

articles.title: US loses measles-free status: Pan American Health Organization (2025)
articles.body:
Washington, D.C., 10 November 2025 (PAHO) –The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced today that the Region of the Americas has lost its verification as free from endemic measles transmission.
The decision follows the conclusion of the PAHO Measles, Rubella, and Congenital Rubella Syndrome Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission, which met in Mexico City from 4 to 7 November 2025 to review the epidemiological situation across the region. The Director of PAHO, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, received and agreed with the Commission’s report indicating that endemic transmission of measles has been reestablished in Canada, where the virus has circulated for at least 12 months.
As a result, the Americas, which was the first region in the world to eliminate measles twice, has now lost its measles-free status. All other countries continue to maintain their measles elimination status.
“This loss represents a setback—but it is also reversible,” said Dr. Barbosa, “Until measles is eliminated worldwide, our Region will continue to face the risk of reintroduction and spread of the virus among unvaccinated or under-vaccinated populations. However, as we have demonstrated before, with political commitment, regional cooperation, and sustained vaccination, the Region can once again interrupt transmission and reclaim this collective achievement.”
Current situation
As of 7 November 2025, 12,596 confirmed measles cases have been reported across ten countries (approximately 95% of the Region’s cases in Canada, Mexico and US), a 30-fold increase compared to 2024. Twenty-eight deaths have been recorded: 23 in Mexico, 3 in the United States, and 2 in Canada.
Active outbreaks are ongoing in Canada, Mexico, the United States, Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, and Belize, mostly triggered by imported cases. Transmission has primarily affected under-vaccinated communities, with 89% of cases occurring in unvaccinated individuals or those with unknown vaccination status. Children under 1 year of age are the most affected, followed by those aged one to four years.
Canada’s measles outbreak began in October 2024 in the province of New Brunswick and has since spread nationwide, with more than 5,000 confirmed cases reported nationwide. Although declining, transmission persists in Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan.
Measles is highly contagious. A single infected person can transmit it to up to 18 others. Severe complications can include pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness, and death. Outbreaks also disrupt daily life and place additional pressure on health systems.
Vaccination remains the most effective means of protection. Over the past 25 years, the measles vaccine has prevented more than six million deaths across the Americas —and an estimated 15 million deaths over the last 50 years. Nevertheless, in 2024, regional coverage for the second dose of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR2) averaged 79%—well below the 95% needed to prevent outbreaks. In addition, only 31% of countries reached 95% or more coverage for the first dose, and just 20% achieved that level for the second dose.
PAHO’s response and recommendations
PAHO continues to provide technical support to countries to strengthen surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, outbreak response, and vaccination campaigns. Experts have been deployed to Mexico, Argentina, and Bolivia, and the organization is monitoring risks in Belize, Brazil and Paraguay.
Dr. Barbosa emphasized: “Every case we prevent, every outbreak we stop saves lives, protects families, and makes communities healthier. Today, rather than lamenting the loss of a regional status, we call on all countries to redouble their efforts to strengthen vaccination rates, surveillance, and timely response to suspected cases—reaching every corner of the Americas. As a Region, we have eliminated measles twice. We can do it a third time.”
RVC strongly encourages countries to:
- Continue strengthening surveillance, immunization and outbreak rapid response activities for every suspect case.
- Expand and consolidate electronic immunization registries across all countries, following PAHO’s established guidelines.
- Maintain sustainable laboratory surveillance by allocating sufficient financial and human resources.
- For suspected cases with clinical and epidemiological risk factors and a negative measles IgM result (with specimens collected within 0–3 days after rash onset), perform PCR testing to confirm or rule out infection.
- Implement all recommendations down to the local level.
- Document outbreak closure following the Regional Framework guidelines.
Looking forward
The Americas have previously faced setbacks, including temporary loss of measles elimination status in Venezuela (2018) and Brazil (2019). The region regained elimination status in 2024 through coordinated regional action.
To regain measles elimination status, a country must demonstrate interruption of endemic transmission for at least 12 consecutive months, supported by comprehensive vaccination, surveillance, and outbreak-response data.
Canada will now present and implement an action plan under PAHO’s regional framework, focused on boosting immunization coverage, reinforcing surveillance systems, and ensuring rapid outbreak response to stop endemic transmission and regaining measles elimination status.
“Cooperation, solidarity, and science are stronger than any virus—because when we work together, we protect the health and lives of all people in the Americas,” Dr. Barbosa concluded.

articles.title: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 483 (I'm Not a Freezer)
articles.body:
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 483 (I'm Not a Freezer)
    
draft-banffy-httpbis-not-a-freezer-00
        This document is an Internet-Draft (I-D).
        Anyone may submit an I-D to the IETF.
        This I-D is not endorsed by the IETF and has no formal standing in the
        IETF standards process.
    
                    
                        draft-banffy-httpbis-not-a-freezer-00
                    
                
Independent Submission                                         R. Bánffy
Internet-Draft                                          15 November 2026
Intended status: Informational                                          
Expires: 19 May 2027
  The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 483 (I'm Not a Freezer)
                 draft-banffy-httpbis-not-a-freezer-00
Abstract
   This document defines the Hypertext Transfer Protocol status code 483
   (I'm Not a Freezer).  A server returns this status code when it
   understands a request that requires freezing or refrigeration
   capabilities but is not capable of providing those capabilities.
   This document also clarifies the distinction between a freezer, a
   refrigerator, a server operating at a low temperature, a frozen
   software process, and an online service advertising "cold storage".
Status of This Memo
   This Internet-Draft is submitted in full conformance with the
   provisions of BCP 78 and BCP 79.
   Internet-Drafts are working documents of the Internet Engineering
   Task Force (IETF).  Note that other groups may also distribute
   working documents as Internet-Drafts.  The list of current Internet-
   Drafts is at https://datatracker.ietf.org/drafts/current/.
   Internet-Drafts are draft documents valid for a maximum of six months
   and may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted by other documents at any
   time.  It is inappropriate to use Internet-Drafts as reference
   material or to cite them other than as "work in progress."
   This Internet-Draft will expire on 19 May 2027.
Copyright Notice
   Copyright (c) 2026 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the
   document authors.  All rights reserved.
   This document is subject to BCP 78 and the IETF Trust's Legal
   Provisions Relating to IETF Documents (https://trustee.ietf.org/
   license-info) in effect on the date of publication of this document.
   Please review these documents carefully, as they describe your rights
   and restrictions with respect to this document.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 1]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
Table of Contents
   1.  Introduction  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   2
   2.  Conventions and Definitions . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   2
   3.  The 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) Status Code . . . . . . . . . . .   3
   4.  Client Behavior . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   4
   5.  Applicability . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   4
   6.  Example: Electronic Mail Concerning Frozen Goods  . . . . . .   5
   7.  Relationship to Status Code 418 . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   6
   8.  Distinguishing Refrigerators from Freezers  . . . . . . . . .   7
   9.  Intermediaries and Cold-Chain Proxies . . . . . . . . . . . .   7
   10. Caching Considerations  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   7
   11. Security Considerations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   8
   12. Privacy Considerations  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   8
   13. IANA Considerations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   9
   14. Implementation Considerations . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   9
   15. Acknowledgments . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .   9
   16. Normative References  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  10
   17. Informative References  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  10
   Author's Address  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  10
1.  Introduction
   HTTP status codes communicate the result of attempting to understand
   and satisfy a request.  Existing status codes cover malformed
   requests, missing resources, unsupported media types, and servers
   that are temporarily unavailable.
   No registered status code clearly indicates that a server understood
   a request but cannot satisfy it because the request requires the
   server to be a freezer.
   This ambiguity can cause clients to repeat requests, select
   inappropriate fallback services, place perishable goods near
   computing equipment, or otherwise confuse information technology
   infrastructure with domestic or industrial refrigeration equipment.
   This document addresses that ambiguity by defining the 483 (I'm Not a
   Freezer) status code.
2.  Conventions and Definitions
   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP
   14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 2]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   Freezer
      An apparatus capable of maintaining its contents at a temperature
      below the freezing point of water for a sustained period.
      Software containers, frozen processes, cold-storage services, and
      servers located in cold climates are not necessarily freezers.
   Refrigerator
      An apparatus that maintains contents below ambient temperature but
      does not necessarily maintain them below the freezing point of
      water.
   Cold storage
      A term that might refer to refrigerated physical storage,
      infrequently accessed data storage, an offline cryptographic
      wallet, or other facilities that are insufficiently warm.  Use of
      the term does not establish freezer capability.
   Freezer-capable server
      An HTTP server associated with equipment that can perform the
      freezing operation requested by the client.  Merely operating
      inside a freezer does not necessarily make an HTTP server freezer-
      capable.
3.  The 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) Status Code
   This document extends the HTTP status-code semantics defined in
   [HTTP] with the 483 (I'm Not a Freezer) status code.  The status code
   indicates that the server understood the request but cannot satisfy
   it because the requested operation requires freezing or refrigeration
   capabilities that the server does not possess.
   A server MAY return 483 when all of the following conditions apply:
   *  The request can be parsed and understood.
   *  Satisfying the request would require the server to freeze,
      refrigerate, chill, or preserve a physical item by reducing its
      temperature.
   *  The server is not capable of performing the requested temperature-
      control operation.
   A server MUST NOT return 483 merely because:
   *  its operating temperature is below ambient temperature;
   *  it uses liquid, air, immersion, or phase-change cooling;
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 3]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   *  it provides a service described as "cold storage";
   *  one or more software processes have been frozen;
   *  its physical location is cold;
   *  its hostname contains words such as "freezer", "ice", "arctic",
      "frost", or "cold"; or
   *  it is unresponsive in a way informally described as "frozen".
   A 483 response SHOULD contain a representation explaining that the
   selected server lacks the required refrigeration capability.  Where
   appropriate, the representation MAY identify a freezer-capable
   alternative.
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: text/plain
   This server is not a freezer and cannot satisfy the requested operation.
4.  Client Behavior
   A client receiving a 483 response SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the
   same request to the same server unless it has reason to believe that
   the server has subsequently acquired suitable refrigeration
   capabilities.
   A client MAY attempt the request against another origin if that
   origin is known to be freezer-capable.
   A client MUST NOT interpret a 483 response as evidence that the
   server is a refrigerator.  The response communicates a lack of
   freezer capability and makes no claim concerning lesser, adjacent, or
   unrelated cooling capabilities.
   Clients SHOULD avoid automatically redirecting physical goods based
   solely on URI authority components, DNS names, electronic mail
   addresses, service banners, or unverified appliance metadata.
5.  Applicability
   Status code 483 is applicable when a request crosses a boundary
   between digital instructions and physical temperature-control
   operations.
   Examples include:
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 4]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   *  an HTTP-controlled kitchen appliance receiving a request to freeze
      food;
   *  an industrial control gateway receiving a request to preserve a
      sample below a specified temperature;
   *  a logistics service receiving an instruction that requires a cold-
      chain facility that it does not operate; and
   *  a general-purpose HTTP server receiving a request intended for a
      refrigeration appliance.
   Status code 483 is not intended to report CPU thermal throttling,
   data-center cooling failures, insufficient heat dissipation,
   unresponsive software, immutable data, object freezing in programming
   languages, or process suspension.
6.  Example: Electronic Mail Concerning Frozen Goods
   Consider an HTTP service that accepts electronic mail for delivery to
   suitable appliances.  A client might inadvertently attempt to deliver
   a message intended for a freezer:
   POST /mail HTTP/1.1
   Host: mail.example
   Content-Type: message/rfc822
   From: alice@example.com
   To: freezer@example.com
   Date: Tue, 3 Nov 2026 10:00:00 +0000
   Message-ID: <peas-483@example.com>
   Subject: Please freeze these peas
   Dear Freezer,
   Please maintain the attached peas at approximately -18 degrees
   Celsius until further notice.
   Regards,
   Alice
   If the selected service is not a freezer and cannot cause the
   requested freezing operation to occur, it MAY reject the request with
   status code 483:
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 5]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: text/plain
   This server is not a freezer and cannot satisfy the requested operation.
   An implementation MUST NOT infer refrigeration capability solely from
   an electronic mail address containing the strings "freezer",
   "refrigerator", "cold", "ice", or similar terminology.
   The recipient address identifies the intended appliance but does not
   prove that the HTTP service handling the message controls that
   appliance.
   The domain names and electronic mail addresses in this example are
   reserved for documentation as described by [RFC2606] and do not
   identify operational refrigeration infrastructure.
7.  Relationship to Status Code 418
   Status code 418 was introduced by the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control
   Protocol [RFC2324] and is associated with an apparatus that is a
   teapot and therefore cannot brew coffee.  Status code 483 represents
   a distinct condition.
   A teapot might be neither a freezer nor a general-purpose server.
   Similarly, a freezer might contain an HTTP server without becoming a
   teapot.
   An implementation choosing between 418 and 483 SHOULD consider the
   immediate reason that the request cannot be satisfied:
   *  If the request cannot be satisfied because the responding
      apparatus is a teapot, 418 might be appropriate.
   *  If the request cannot be satisfied because the responding server
      is not a freezer, 483 might be appropriate.
   *  If the apparatus is both a teapot and not a freezer, the
      implementation SHOULD report the condition most directly relevant
      to the requested operation.
   This document does not define response prioritization for combination
   refrigerator-freezer-teapot appliances.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 6]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
8.  Distinguishing Refrigerators from Freezers
   A refrigerator is not necessarily a freezer.  An implementation MUST
   NOT advertise freezer capability merely because it can maintain a
   temperature lower than the surrounding environment.
   If a request specifies a target temperature, the server SHOULD
   evaluate its actual supported temperature range.  A server that can
   maintain 4 degrees Celsius but cannot maintain -18 degrees Celsius
   can return 483 when asked to preserve frozen food at -18 degrees
   Celsius.
   This document does not allocate a separate status code meaning "I'm
   Only a Refrigerator".  Such allocation is left for future work,
   preferably after an appropriate cooling-off period.
9.  Intermediaries and Cold-Chain Proxies
   An intermediary MUST NOT replace a 483 response with a success
   response unless it has arranged for the requested operation to be
   performed by a freezer-capable service.
   An intermediary that forwards a request to a freezer-capable service
   SHOULD preserve sufficient request information to maintain
   traceability through the cold chain.
   A proxy MUST NOT claim that a request has been frozen merely because
   it has been buffered, queued, archived, or stored on media described
   as cold storage.
   Intermediaries SHOULD NOT select a refrigeration service based only
   on the service name.  Capability claims ought to be authenticated
   before perishable or temperature-sensitive goods are redirected.
10.  Caching Considerations
   A 483 response is not heuristically cacheable.
   A 483 response can be cached when explicit freshness information
   permits caching, subject to [HTTP-CACHING].
   Implementations ought to use short freshness lifetimes when
   refrigeration capabilities can change.  A server might acquire
   freezer capability through appliance discovery, configuration,
   repair, attachment of suitable hardware, or relocation.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 7]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   A cache MUST include relevant request-selection information in its
   cache key when freezer capability depends on the requested product,
   target temperature, duration, physical location, or other request
   characteristics.
11.  Security Considerations
   A 483 response can disclose information about the physical
   capabilities of a server, appliance, building, warehouse, or
   logistics network.  Such information might assist an attacker in
   identifying facilities that lack refrigeration capability.
   Servers SHOULD avoid disclosing unnecessary details about appliance
   models, internal temperatures, stored contents, physical locations,
   maintenance schedules, or cold-chain topology.
   A malicious service might falsely claim freezer capability in order
   to receive physical goods, operational instructions, or sensitive
   inventory information.  Clients SHOULD authenticate services before
   relying on claims of refrigeration capability.
   Implementations MUST NOT treat the presence or absence of a 483
   response as proof that a physical item has been frozen, refrigerated,
   preserved, spoiled, thawed, or consumed.
   Request bodies associated with freezing operations might reveal
   dietary preferences, medical requirements, biological sample
   information, commercial inventory, or other sensitive data.
   Implementations SHOULD apply suitable confidentiality and access-
   control protections.
   Operators are advised not to troubleshoot servers by placing them
   inside domestic freezers.  Condensation, restricted airflow, thermal
   shock, and the objections of other freezer occupants can produce
   undesirable results.
12.  Privacy Considerations
   Requests involving refrigeration can expose information about food,
   medicine, scientific samples, commercial shipments, or household
   activity.  Servers SHOULD minimize the information returned in a 483
   response and SHOULD avoid echoing sensitive request content.
   Logs containing 483 responses SHOULD be protected according to the
   sensitivity of associated request metadata and content.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 8]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
13.  IANA Considerations
   This document requests that IANA register the following entry in the
   "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Code Registry":
               +=======+===================+===============+
               | Value | Description       | Reference     |
               +=======+===================+===============+
               | 483   | I'm Not a Freezer | This document |
               +-------+-------------------+---------------+
                    Table 1: Requested HTTP Status Code
                                Registration
   If the registration request is not approved, this section can itself
   be considered safely stored for future use, although not necessarily
   below freezing.
14.  Implementation Considerations
   Implementers are encouraged to use the exact reason phrase "I'm Not a
   Freezer" when a reason phrase is supported.  Clients MUST NOT depend
   on the reason phrase because HTTP semantics are identified by the
   numeric status code.
   Protocol versions that do not transmit a reason phrase can use status
   code 483 without modification.
   Implementations MAY include a machine-readable problem detail
   describing the unsupported refrigeration operation, subject to
   [RFC9457].
   HTTP/1.1 483 I'm Not a Freezer
   Content-Type: application/problem+json
   Cache-Control: no-store
   {
     "type": "https://example.com/problems/not-a-freezer",
     "title": "I'm Not a Freezer",
     "status": 483,
     "detail": "The requested temperature is outside supported capabilities."
   }
15.  Acknowledgments
   The author thanks the designers of HTTP, refrigeration equipment,
   electronic mail, and combination appliances for creating the
   conditions that made this clarification necessary.
Banffy                     Expires 19 May 2027                  [Page 9]
Internet-Draft              I'm Not a Freezer              November 2026
   The peas used in the example were not harmed during preparation of
   this document, although their final temperature could not be
   independently verified.
16.  Normative References
   [RFC2119]  Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate
              Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119,
              DOI 10.17487/RFC2119, March 1997,
