articles.title: How Will AI Affect Open Source Development?
articles.body:
How Will AI Affect Open Source Development? (linuxfoundation.org) 12
			
		 	
				This week the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) announced it would broaden its AI security resources, including a new guide to finding and fixing vulnerabilities using AI, "from preparing and sandboxing AI to validating, fixing, and preventing issues."  The guide "stresses that AI-generated patches should never be trusted without automated tests and human review. An online course (LFD126) is planned for the coming months."
OpenSSF also released the State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026 report (supported by OpenSSF, ActiveState and the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation). And it turns out the 2026 report "found a growing gap between the pace of AI-driven software development and organizations' ability to secure the code being produced."
 58% of surveyed teams ship code faster than security reviews can keep up, while 60% say AI coding assistants have increased the number of external packages in their codebases. This data underscores the importance of trusted, reliable guidance as AI deployment continues to grow. 
Meanwhile the Linux Foundation announced at this week's Web Summit that it was releasing a new study on "how commercial open source companies generate revenue, convert users into customers and build their businesses," emphasizing the question's new relevance in the age of AI.  "AI now writes code almost for free, and that raises a hard question for the whole software industry: if code costs next to nothing, where does the value of software lie?"
Commercial open source [COSS] companies have been answering that question for more than 30 years. They have built large businesses on code they give away, which makes them a good guide to how software will make money in the age of AI...  Seventy-two percent of respondents report a net positive impact from AI, against 8% negative. So far, the gains show up mostly inside companies. Internal productivity is the most cited benefit (73%), ahead of market expansion (46%) and new monetization opportunities (39%). AI roles are the only hiring category growing on net.
COSS strategy is mostly unchanged by AI. But when companies do adapt, they are nearly twice as likely to open more of their core product rather than become more closed.  When asked what sets them apart, 57% of companies name brand recognition and trust, well ahead of enterprise features, integrations and community size. They turn that trust into revenue through support and services (63%), managed cloud (49%) and open core (43%). Most combine these: 65% run two or more revenue models. 
Companies stack models as they grow, rather than switching between them: managed cloud rises from 35% of companies below $5 million ARR to 66% above $20 million. Venture-backed companies lean toward open core (53% vs. 38% for others). 
The report draws on a survey of 225 commercial open source founders and enterprise leaders (published by Linux Foundation Research in partnership with Serena,  and with sponsorship from AWS, Red Hat, Futurewei and the  Cloud Native Computing Foundation.  And when it comes to open source, "over half of founders point to brand recognition and community trust as their greatest asset," said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.  So
"The findings from this year's report prove that AI isn't a threat to commercial open source software — it's an accelerating tailwind.  With 72% of companies viewing AI as a net positive primarily driving internal productivity, the ecosystem is leaning further into collaboration." 
The Linux Foundation's announcement includes an interesting perspective from Matthieu Lavergne, partner at the venture capital company Serena.  "Open source won the developer. Next, it will win the agent. The 225 founders we surveyed mostly see AI as a productivity gain today, but that's only the start: agents are set to become open source's largest users, and they choose what is open, proven and trusted. The founders who build and price for these new users will define the infrastructure of the AI era."

articles.title: Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China?
articles.body:
Did Alice Huang's Megaspeed Bypass America's Controls on Exporting Nvidia Chip to China? (cnn.com) 29
			
		 	
				In three years "Megaspeed International" went from from inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary "to one of Asia's biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US," reports CNN.
"It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks," trade data investigator William George told CNN. 
As Nvidia's Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, "Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia," CNN writes, noting scrutiny of the company from the Singapore government and US officials "concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers..."
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia's most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China's tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.  US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those...   [T]rade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia... Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year... 
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company's server purchases and their final destinations.   In a statement, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence that Huang had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information "to downplay her role" at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws. A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.  
CNN reminds readers that Jensen Huang accompanied US President Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, and also lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports.  "The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue."
"However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well," they add.  And the Taiwanese government is even seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, "as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong."

articles.title: Show HN: Turbo-Browser-MCP – Batch forms, DOM deltas and submit guards for MCP
articles.body:
turbo-browser-mcp is a Playwright-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) server built to cut LLM token waste and multi-turn latency in browser automation. It consolidates 25-33 fine-grained browser primitives into 10 batched tools featuring delta DOM snapshots, single-turn React/Shadow DOM/iframe form prefill, direct disk file uploads (no Base64 in context), parallel tab sessions, network blocking presets, and a default human-in-the-loop Submit guard.
All figures below come from benchmarks/benchmark.mjs (npm run benchmark) running headless Chromium locally with exact OpenAI o200k_base tokenization (tiktoken 0.14.0):
Note on latency vs LLM inference turns: Eliminating 10 round-trips on a 10-field form saves both 7x in browser execution (574 ms -> 82 ms) and 10 separate LLM inference round-trips (2-5s per turn in agent loops) plus ~71,800 replayed history tokens.
Standard MCP servers charge an LLM round-trip for every snapshot, field fill, <select> choice, upload, and verification check. Each turn re-sends the growing conversation history back into the model.
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Agent as LLM Agent
    participant Std as Standard MCP (Playwright / DevTools)
    participant Turbo as turbo-browser-mcp
    Note over Agent,Std: Standard MCP (12+ LLM turns, full ARIA tree + history replay each step)
    Agent->>Std: 1. snapshot() -> full ARIA (~3,568 tok)
    loop Repeats 10+ times across fields, selects, checkboxes, upload
        Agent->>Std: fill / select_option / click
        Std-->>Agent: full ARIA or confirmation re-added to history
    end
    Agent->>Std: 12. upload inline or click chooser
    Note over Agent,Turbo: turbo-browser-mcp (2 LLM turns total, delta & inline snapshot)
    Agent->>Turbo: 1. inspect_compact(mode: "forms") -> compact refs (1,135 tok)
    Agent->>Turbo: 2. smart_fill_form(fields: [...10 fields + disk PDF...], returnSnapshot: true)
    Turbo-->>Agent: Filled 10 fields + guarded before Submit + inline snapshot (811 tok)
    - 4 connection modes (--mode auto|cdp|persistent|launch):
  - auto (default): probes --cdp http://127.0.0.1:9222 first so agents can reuse an existing signed-in browser session, then falls back to launching Chromium.
  - cdp: attach directly to a running Chromium/Chrome/Edge remote debugging port.
  - persistent: launch with a reusable --user-data-dir profile across runs.
  - launch: start a clean browser session (--headless by default, or --headed).
- Auto binary discovery (src/playwright-loader.mjs): checks playwright-core cache revisions across Windows, macOS, and Linux, system installs of Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Brave, and Chromium, or an explicit --executable <path>.
- Per-tab isolation (tabs_batch): open tabs inside named isolatedContext sandboxes with separate cookies and storage, batch-open up to 10 concurrent URLs (open_many), activate, reload, go back/forward, resize viewport, and emulate colorScheme, media, reducedMotion, contrast, forcedColors, or custom userAgent.
- Snapshot modes: interactive, forms, article, and all.
- Cross-boundary traversal: flattens main frame DOM, child iframes (includeFrames, frameIdx), and open Shadow DOM. Injects an init script hooking Element.prototype.attachShadow (WeakMap + WeakRef/FinalizationRegistry + window.__tbmGetShadowRoot) to keep post-init closed Shadow roots inspectable and guarded, traverses <slot> assignedNodes({ flatten: true }), and supports Form-Associated Custom Elements.
- Token controls: onlyChanged: true emits only elements added or changed since the prior snapshot; query filters by regex or substring; boxes: true adds [box=x,y,w,h] only when needed; maxChars caps payload size; savePath writes full output to disk.
Prefills an entire form in one MCP call while flushing microtasks and macrotasks between controlled inputs:
- Standard & framework inputs: text, email, password, number, date, textarea, <input type="range">, checkboxes, radio groups (check, not, overwrite). Triggers React-controlled state updates via native property setters and synthetic events.
- Selects & custom widgets: <select> and <select multiple> (option / values), ARIA comboboxes, ARIA switches, contenteditable rich editors, and Gmail compose dialogs (gmail: { to, subject, body }).
- Frame & wildcard targeting: target specific iframes via frameIdx, or set all: true to populate matching controls across frames.
- Direct disk uploads: pass file or files paths directly to Playwright setInputFiles without loading binary files or Base64 strings into LLM context.
- Atomic verification: pass returnSnapshot: true to inspect the updated form state in the same tool response.
- act_fast actions: click, dblclick, hover, focus, clear, fill, type (slowly, delayMs, submit), select, check, uncheck, drag, drop (file, files, or custom MIME dropData), press (key + modifiers: Alt, Control, ControlOrMeta, Meta, Shift), scroll (dx, dy), wait (ms, state, loadState, text, textGone, url), and upload.
- Targeting options: compact [eN] ref, CSS selector, visible text, label, or viewport (x, y) coordinates, with button (left, right, middle) and frameIdx.
- batch_actions: runs an ordered list of DOM actions and nested smart_fill_form steps in one MCP call, stopping safely if blocked by the Submit guard or optionally continuing on step errors (continueOnError).
- extract_clean_text: extracts readable plain text or compact Markdown (format: "text" | "markdown") from main/article containers and iframes, stripped of script and style noise.
- evaluate_js: runs JS expressions or (el, arg) element functions in any frame (frameIdx) with JSON-serialized results and optional savePath export.
- capture_page: full-page or element-scoped screenshots (png or jpeg with quality, css or device scale, optional returnImage) and PDF generation saved to a confined savePath.
- network_session presets: turbo, no-images, no-media, and clean (unblock all), alongside custom blockResources and blockUrls patterns.
- Session & storage management: read/write/clear browser cookies, localStorage/sessionStorage, and export or reload full Playwright storageState JSON files (saveStorageStatePath, loadStorageStatePath).
- page_diagnostics: defaults to errors-only (level: "errors", statusFilter: "errors") to surface failures cleanly without flooding context, while supporting all, includeStatic, urlFilter, deep request/response inspection (reqId + part), completed downloads, and dialog auto-handling (dialogPolicy: accept/dismiss).
Run the benchmark suite yourself with Chromium and Playwright installed:
npm run benchmark
Environment & methodology: Headless Chromium via playwright-core, counting exact OpenAI o200k_base tokens via Python tiktoken (approx-bpe fallback if tiktoken is unavailable). Cumulative workflow tokens model standard chat-history replay across $N$ sequential turns: $\sum_{i=1}^{N} (N - i + 1) \cdot T_i$, plus a one-shot baseline where the first turn captures context before acting.
Measured against installed MCP JSON schemas on disk (compact parameter schemas without annotations):
v0.5.0 added wait_for_human and the commit-safety parameters for about 160 tokens per turn (v0.4.0: 3,010 compact). To keep that small, expect / submissionKey / allowDuplicate are declared only on batch_actions (a one-step batch works for a single click), and the network guard is switched on by environment variable, so it costs no schema tokens. The label lists for other languages run inside the page and are never sent to the model.
When to keep Chrome DevTools MCP alongside turbo-browser-mcp: chrome-devtools-mcp provides Lighthouse audits, performance trace analysis, CSS computed style panels, and V8 heap snapshots. turbo-browser-mcp focuses on fast multi-step UI automation, forms, and scraping with minimal token overhead.
- Human-in-the-loop Submit Guard (allowSubmit=false by default):
  - smart_fill_form (stopBeforeSubmit: true), act_fast, and batch_actions inspect matching elements, W3C AccName labels (isSafeSubmitter), implicit HTML form Enter submissions, key chords (Shift+Enter, Enter+Shift), HTMLFormElement.prototype.submit/requestSubmit, and same-origin iframe contentWindow/contentDocument proxies.
  - Final actions resembling Submit, Publish, Send, Post, Apply, Confirm, or payment triggers are blocked unless allowSubmit: true is explicitly passed or --allow-submit is enabled at startup.
  - Trade-off: pre-existing closed Shadow roots on already-open CDP tabs (attached before the init script ran) or strict cross-origin sandboxed frames fall back to Playwright frame handles, coordinate actions, and keyboard input.
- Workspace Path Confinement (TURBO_BROWSER_SAVE_ROOT):
  - File outputs (savePath, saveStorageStatePath) and state inputs (loadStorageStatePath) are strictly confined to the current working directory or TURBO_BROWSER_SAVE_ROOT.
  - Lexical checks, lstatSync/readlinkSync symlink verification, and realpathSync validation block .. traversal, UNC network paths, dangling symlinks, cyclic symlinks, and Windows junctions before reading or writing.
Readers who run agents on real portals pointed out three gaps in a label-based guard. v0.5.0 adds an opt-in answer to each. expect, submissionKey and allowDuplicate appear in the batch_actions schema; act_fast accepts the same arguments without advertising them. The network guard is turned on with TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD=true and covers act_fast, batch_actions and smart_fill_form.
- A landed click is not a confirmed submission → expect. After an allowed submit, pass expect: { urlMatches?, textMatches?, selector?, timeoutMs? }. The result carries submitVerified and evidence (the new URL, a text snippet such as a receipt number, or the matched selector). If nothing shows up in time you get submitVerified: false and a reason, so the agent does not report "done" on an empty submission list.
- A re-run is a second entry, not a retry → submissionKey. With submissionKey: "portal:2026-11-15:entry-42", every allowed submit is appended to a JSONL ledger (~/.turbo-browser-mcp/submissions.jsonl, or TURBO_BROWSER_LEDGER, or ledgerPath inside the save root). A later call with the same key is refused with blockedBy: "ledger" unless allowDuplicate: true.
- Labels lie → modal rule + networkGuard. On many Korean portals the last step reads 다음 and the real commit is a 확인 inside a modal that opens afterwards.
  - Affirmative buttons (확인, OK, Yes, Confirm, 確認, 确定, Đồng ý, …) inside dialog / [role=dialog] / [role=alertdialog] / [aria-modal=true] now count as commits (blockedBy: "modal"). Cookie banners (dialog text mentions cookies) and date/time pickers (dialog contains a calendar grid or date input) are excluded; a confirmation that only mentions "privacy" or "consent" is still blocked.
  - When an action makes the page call form.submit() / requestSubmit() or fire a submit event and the guard stops it, the result now says so (submitSuppressed, note) instead of a bare ok: true. The action itself (a select, a check) still counts as done, so batches continue.
  - Common Korean, Japanese, Chinese and Vietnamese submit labels were added (제출, 신청, 등록, 결제, 送信, 確定, 提交, Hoàn tất, …), and 다음, 次へ, 下一步 are treated like Next.
  - TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD=true is the safety net that does not depend on labels: while submitting is not allowed, non-GET navigations and same-site fetch/XHR POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE are stopped and reported (blockedBy: "network", networkBlocked[]). Blocked navigations get a 204 so the page and the half-filled form stay put. Let harmless endpoints through with TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD_ALLOW="/autosave$,/analytics". Per call, the undeclared arguments networkGuard, networkGuardAllow and networkGuardSettleMs override the env values. It is off by default because multi-step wizards often POST on every "Next".
  - Every blocked result now says which mechanism stopped it: blockedBy is label, modal, network or ledger.
Limits:
- The network guard watches the action plus networkGuardSettleMs (250 ms) afterwards, so a commit fired later by a timer is not caught. WebSocket messages, requests made by a service worker, and cross-site fetch POSTs are not inspected (cross-site navigations are). Patterns in TURBO_BROWSER_NETWORK_GUARD_ALLOW are split on commas, so a pattern cannot contain one.
- The ledger is written only when the call returns. If the call throws after the page already sent the submission (for example a navigation timeout), nothing is recorded; check the site before re-running.
- expect.selector that is not a valid selector never matches, so the call reports submitVerified: false after the timeout.
Some sites fail their bot check whenever the browser is remote-controlled, so a person has to open the same profile in a normal browser first. turbo-browser-mcp does not try to hide automation: no stealth plugins, no fingerprint or navigator.webdriver patching, no CAPTCHA solving. It supports two hand-off flows instead.
- Before the session: turbo-browser-mcp --open-profile --url https://site.example/login opens plain Chrome (no debugging port, no automation flags) on the dedicated profile ~/.turbo-browser-mcp/chrome-profile (or --user-data-dir). The human logs in or passes the check and closes the window. Then start the server with --user-data-dir <same path> or --launch-chrome, and the agent reuses those cookies. This works for sites that check at login; a site that re-checks on every request will still see an automated browser.
- During the session: the agent calls wait_for_human with a message and a condition (urlMatches, selector, textMatches or textGone). The tool brings the tab to the front and polls until the condition holds, then the agent continues in the same tab with the same cookies. Keep timeoutMs below your MCP client's request timeout and call it again to keep waiting.
{
  "name": "wait_for_human",
  "arguments": {
    "message": "Please sign in and finish the security check, then leave the tab open.",
    "selector": "#account-menu",
    "timeoutMs": 120000
  }
}{
  "name": "batch_actions",
  "arguments": {
    "steps": [
      { "action": "smart_fill_form", "fields": [{ "selector": "#name", "value": "홍길동" }] },
      { "action": "click", "text": "다음" },
      { "action": "click", "text": "확인" }
    ],
    "allowSubmit": true,
    "expect": { "textMatches": "접수번호\\s*R-\\d+", "timeoutMs": 8000 },
    "submissionKey": "photo-contest:2026-11-15:entry-1"
  }
}{
  "name": "smart_fill_form",
  "arguments": {
    "fields": [
      { "selector": "#full_name", "value": "Alex Nguyen" },
      { "selector": "#email", "value": "alex@example.com" },
      { "selector": "#country", "option": "United States" },
      { "selector": "#skills", "values": ["TypeScript", "Playwright"] },
      { "selector": "#agree_terms", "check": true },
      { "selector": "#resume_pdf", "file": "./assets/resume.pdf" }
    ],
    "stopBeforeSubmit": true,
    "returnSnapshot": true
  }
}{
  "name": "inspect_compact",
  "arguments": {
    "mode": "interactive",
    "onlyChanged": true,
    "maxChars": 3000
  }
}{
  "name": "tabs_batch",
  "arguments": {
    "operations": [
      { "action": "open", "url": "https://example.com/app", "isolatedContext": "acct-a" },
      { "action": "open_many", "urls": ["https://example.com/docs", "https://example.com/pricing"], "concurrency": 4 }
    ]
  }
}git clone https://github.com/Tthanh2k6/turbo-browser-mcp.git
cd turbo-browser-mcp
npm install
npm run doctor
If you need Playwright's bundled Chromium (or have no system Chrome/Edge/Brave installed):
npx playwright-core install chromium
Using local clone:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "turbo-browser": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/turbo-browser-mcp/src/index.mjs"],
      "env": {
        "TURBO_BROWSER_SAVE_ROOT": "/absolute/path/to/allowed/workspace"
      }
    }
  }
}
Using npx / binary entrypoint:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "turbo-browser": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "turbo-browser-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
In Chrome 136+/144+, enabling chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging on the default User Data directory exposes a WebSocket in DevToolsActivePort that displays an "Allow remote debugging?" prompt whenever a new WebSocket client connects. turbo-browser-mcp provides two built-in solutions so overnight AFK multi-agent runs never hang on a prompt:
- Automatic CDP Keep-Alive Bridge Daemon (npm run bridge / --bridge, enabled automatically on DevToolsActivePort):
  - Spawns a detached background multiplexer (src/cdp-bridge.mjs on http://127.0.0.1:9224) that holds one persistent upstream WebSocket to Chrome open indefinitely and intercepts Browser.close so downstream scripts never terminate your browser.
  - You click Allow once when starting your session; afterwards, any number of MCP servers, CLI scripts, or subagents can connect and disconnect all night with 0 additional prompts.
- Zero-Prompt Dedicated Profile Launcher (npm run launch-chrome / --launch-chrome):
  - Launches Chrome with --remote-debugging-port=9222 and a dedicated --user-data-dir (~/.turbo-browser-mcp/chrome-profile), where Chrome exposes standard HTTP/WS CDP with 0 confirmation dialogs even on the very first connection.
npm test            # 424 passing tests across 87 suites (27 test files under test/*.test.mjs)
npm run doctor      # Environment check for Node, Playwright, Chromium, and CDP
npm run bridge      # Start/verify persistent CDP Keep-Alive Bridge daemon
npm run benchmark   # Local Chromium speed & exact o200k_base token benchmark
npm run benchmark:e2e  # End-to-end wizard task + commit-safety cases (see benchmarks/E2E_COMPARISON.md)
Tested automatically on GitHub Actions (ubuntu-latest) across Node 20 and Node 22.

articles.title: The 'europoors' rants reflect an American insecurity
articles.body:
There’s a particularly virulent strand of column-publishing and Twitter/X debate happening right now which, if it continues, will require me to seek medical attention for perpetual eye roll. It consists of American and British people gleefully writing about America’s explosive economic growth at the moment, and comparing it to Europe’s sluggish post-Covid recovery. Everyone seems to have their own opinion explaining the difference, the most convincing of which I find the idea that the EU has stuck with conservative neoliberal orthodoxies for the economy while America has been quietly more flexible.
On Twitter, these columns have then translated to a bunch of reply guys (it’s always men) gloating about the American economy and mocking the “europoors” who live in abject poverty while enviously looking across the Atlantic. Life is much better in America, they insist, because they have tumble dryers, bigger houses, bigger cars, higher salaries and, of course, freedom. These messages are not only coming from Americans but also from Brits - and it feels to me like the genesis for this is coming more from the latter than the former. There’s a particular strain of Tory Britain-bashing America-obsessed London elite, in the mould of Dan Hannan, who seem to think they are Americans born in the wrong body.
As someone who grew up in the US and moved to Europe at age 26, I could go on with a nuanced take about the positives and negatives of each. I’ll leave that to others. What I find much more interesting is why we’re getting this sudden rush of America-gloating and Europoor-bashing at this particular moment. This conversation isn’t being sparked in the EU. All of these Twitter flare-ups are started by people in Britain or America, and when people in the EU reply to point out that what they’re saying is nonsense, it’s “cope from pathetic europoors”. In other words, this isn’t a two-way dialogue. This is a man draped in red, white and blue standing on a soapbox on the street and screaming at European passers-by, who occasionally stop to challenge him.
Why have Americans suddenly become so insecure about their own supposed greatness? 20 years ago it would have just been taken as a given that life in America is better than life in Europe - also by most Europeans. For Americans, Europe was a holiday destination, not a real place with real economies who might compete with the mighty US. I can attest to this from personal experience. When I emigrated in 2006, Americans couldn’t really wrap their heads around what I was doing. My last job in the US was TV and radio reporting covering the US Congress in Washington. During that time I read Jeremy Rifkin’s The European Dream and it inspired me to move to Europe. My intention then, as it remains, was to do a permanent move for a better life. Since the US has no history of emigration like European countries do, people couldn’t quite understand this concept. They would get it if I was taking some time off to go live the wine and cheese life for awhile. They could understand it if my job was temporarily transferring me to Europe for a few years (as some of my friends and family have done). They could not understand the idea that I would choose to immigrate to Europe, without a job (or, at the time, a European passport), in search of a better life. This had always only happened in the other direction, as my Italian Great Grandfather did in 1916. 90 years later after his boat trip across the Atlantic, I used Italy’s strange ancestry citizenship policy to get myself an EU passport through him. If you had told him then that his great grandson would use his Italian roots to emigrate the other way to improve his life, he probably wouldn’t have believed you.
But now, 20 years later, my friends and family get it. Since 2016, as the United States seems to drift closer and closer to democratic collapse, I keep being told during my biannual visits to my country of birth that they are envious. My peers my age who I graduated high school and college with (a lot of whom, I can tell you candidly, are pretty damn miserable), say they wish they had made the move when they could have when they were younger. We all grew up being told that America is the best country on earth, that all other countries are living in squalor and we’re so lucky to have been born where we were. I’ve had experiences of American visitors coming to Europe for the first time feeling shocked and confused to find that so many things are more developed than in the US.
For years, Europeans also operated under the assumption that life in America was better than in Europe. Growing up on a continent dominated by American culture, they have been inundated with idealized Hollywood images of how great life in the US is. When I moved from New York City to London in 2006 I heard a constant response of “but why would you come here?” Ditto for when I later moved to Paris and Brussels. The people saying this had no experience of living in America themselves (or, often, even visiting). They were basing their assumption that life must be better there based on the television, movies and music they have been surrounded by their whole lives. Over the years many Europeans have told me they dream of one day winning the “green card lottery” to win a chance to live in America, as if it’s a prize. It’s a system that is incredibly insulting to Europeans, but for decades in the European mind it made sense.
However over the past ten years I’ve noticed this perception has been slowly changing here in Europe, and it’s also starting to change in America. No longer is the starting assumption point that America is great and Europe is inferior. Americans have started to wake up to the economic power of the European Union, which is now a larger market than the US. The spread of English as Europe’s lingua franca, at the same time that social media has connected the world, has also enabled more communication across the Atlantic. For the first time, Europeans have started to see the truth about life in America. And even though the US remains in a cultural bubble (media goes out but rarely comes in) and Americans don’t see much of the outside world, they are still starting to see glimpses of what daily life (not vacations) in Europe is really like. They can see on social media that people actually live pretty happy lives. That they’re given at least 20 days vacation per year (the legal EU minimum) as opposed to the usual five in America. That they’re able to attend university for free or next-to-nothing and start their careers without student debt. That they don’t need to worry about healthcare costs. That they can live comfortably without owning a car. That they enjoy social protections which guarantee them a good quality of life.
The opening of that window into what life is like in Europe seems to be making certain people in America (and their admirers in Britain) very defensive. But there is another, larger reason why these people are lashing out at the “europoors” in this defensive way right now. They can see that both Britain and America, once the envy of the world, have now become internationally renowned basket cases. Americans are now living with the knowledge that half their fellow citizens either support a Trump dictatorship or are indifferent to it. They are living with the anxiety that comes from living in a country that could, at any moment, slip into civil war. Brits, on the other hand, are living with the humiliations of Brexit’s effects on their economy and society. They have been reduced to a country with an Italian-style revolving door of prime ministers, the most recent former one reduced to hawking upside-down books on US cable news to anchors who don’t seem to even know who they are. This humiliation is a national trauma, there is no other way to describe it. And many are lashing out as a result. They’re defending the American horse they bet on in 2016, and feel the constant need to demonize and denigrate the EU horse they sold. And because the American media still gets so much of its knowledge about Europe via the biased British prism, the discourse in the US has become infected by the UK’s post-Brexit trauma.
To put it bluntly, 20 years ago Europe was an afterthought for Americans - an irrelevant Disneyland. That they are suddenly paying so much attention to it, even to denigrate it, shouldn’t get under our skin. It comes from a place of fragility, of psychological trauma. It is their problem, not ours.
Postscript
I know I said I wouldn’t get into a debate about the pros and cons of Europe and America, but I do want to say one thing about this “higher salaries” thing that I keep hearing Europeans talk about. Yes, net salaries in wealthy areas of the US are much higher than in wealthy areas of Europe, largely because of the drastically lower tax rate. But if you’re just comparing the headline figure, it’s giving you a misleading impression of people’s disposable income. Subtract from that monthly net the monthly healthcare co-pay even when you have insurance through your company (mine at my last US job was $400/month), your student loan repayments (mine are still $300/month), your car and fuel costs (New York City is the only place you can get by without a car), and various other costs that would be provided by the state in Europe such as childcare. And when it comes to those super-high salaries in New York City or Washington I keep seeing people talk about, go have a look at average rental prices in those cities and you might understand why my friends who live there have far far less disposable income than I do, even though on paper it might look like they’re making more.

articles.title: Hundreds of Fake Accounts Defended Jensen Huang On Social Media
articles.body:
Hundreds of Fake Accounts Defended Jensen Huang On Social Media (msn.com) 62
			
		 	
				The Washington Post reports on something peculiar about support for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang online after he'd told the world he'd been unfaithful to his wife (before reports of his second extramarital affair):
Joining the chorus online were voices of seemingly everyday people: a chef, a stock trader, a Hebrew teacher and several environmental activists. But at least 400 of them were fake, according to research from the nonprofit Midas Project, with links to a public relations firm involved in previous so-called "sockpuppet" campaigns...  Many of the fake accounts, according to Midas Project executive director Tyler Johnston, replied to journalists, former U.S. officials and other prominent figures and backed not just Huang but Nvidia's push to sell its cutting-edge chips to Chinese firms. 
Like other documented influence campaigns, the posts appeared to have limited reach; the most-viewed tweet garnered about 8,000 views and 32 likes.  Still, some of the posts targeted lawmakers, including accounts for the [U.S.] House Select Committee on China, Republicans on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts). "That's a place where you might not need a lot of views, but maybe the staffers who are running the lawmakers' account are paying attention to how their messages are received," said Johnston, whose group advocates for safe AI development...
There were other clues that helped identify accounts as being part of an apparently coordinated campaign, according to the Midas Project. Some of them were created minutes or hours apart, and had user names and profile photos refreshed at similar times. They also sometimes engaged on oddly specific issues ranging from Qatar to Nippon Steel's bid for U.S. Steel and a waste management plant in Oregon.... Any one one of the posts — often replies to other posts — might have not looked suspicious in isolation. But the various clues taken together, Johnston said, gave evidence that they were linked. Some of the accounts then rushed to delete posts after he posted his findings online, and at least 260 of them have been deactivated or suspended by X.

articles.title: Book list for streetfighting computer scientists
articles.body:
Book list for streetfighting computer scientists
2025 edition. this is very different from most "best books for programmers" lists you'll see, with Code Complete and Clean Code and Wistful Wanking for Practical Wankers and Design Slatterns and titles like that. you'll figure all that out as you go along. these are books to read so that you can cut motherfuckers with knives. do you need to read all of these? only if you want to know the things inside, i guess.
Introductory streetfighting
- Stepanov, From Mathematics to Generic Programming and The Elements of Programming
- Gustedt, Modern C
- Hanson, C Interfaces and Implementations
- Stroustrup, The C++ Programming Language
- Josuttis, C++ Move Semantics, because a language feature requiring 200 pages of explication is worth studying? no, because this book justifies Rust better than any text on that language.
- Klabnik, Nichols, and Krycho, The Rust Programming Language
need you write in C or C++? not generally. but they are a lingua franca, implemented on most hardware you'll meet, and serve as the native API expression of all operating system that matter. rust is a pretty good language to write and read, and much less to talk about all the fucking time, so cut that shit out.
Brawling combat
- Dijkstra, A Discipline of Programming. the most beautiful book, page-for-page, in all of computer science.
- Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, especially volumes 1 and 4B, third edition
- Warren, Hacker's Delight. make sure you get the second edition
- Stevens and Rago, Advanced Programming in the UNIX Environment, get at least the second and preferably the third edition
- Stevens, UNIX Network Programming, second edition
- Abelson + Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, best cover on a CS textbook hands down, second edition
- Varghese, Networking Algorithmics
- McKusick, The Design and Implementation of the FreeBSD Operating System
- Kerrisk, The Linux Programming Interface
- Garcia + Widjaja, Communications Networks. do you even ARQ, bro?
- Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, especially volume 1. this is why they made you take prob/stats.
- Hennessy + Paterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. the older editions don't lock material away from you online, but are...older.
- Kennedy, Optimizing Compilers for Modern Architectures. if you want to actually implement compilers make sure you get Muchnik's Advanced Compiler Design and Implmentation as well
- CLRS, Introduction to Algorithms
- Samet, Metric and Multidimensional Data Structures
- McKenney, Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It? despite its preposterous title, this book is excellent, and covers things you won't find anywhere else. If Naming Books is so Hard for You, Why Didn't You Ask For Help?
- Crochemere et al, Algorithms on Strings. just as french as it sounds, a true force de frappe
- Culler et al, Parallel Computer Architecture
- Ward + Halstead, Computation Structures
- Shriver + Smith, The Anatomy of a High-Performance Microprocessor
- Vazirani, Approximation Algorithms
- Raghaven + Motwani, Randomized Algorithms
- Garey and Johnson, Computers and Intractability. it's always embarrassing to realize you've promised a solution to an np-complete problem.
- Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation. but not as embarrassing as realizing you've promised a solution to an undecidable problem. also, the pumping lemma!
- Galub + Van Loan, Matrix Computations. this is pretty much a straight mathematics textbook, but roaming multiethnic gangs of matrices make up many streetfights.
For the advanced streetfighter
- Ahora + Barak, Computational Complexity
- Pierce, Types and Programming Languages
- Okasaki, Purely Functional Data Structures
- Van Roy + Hardidi, Concepts, Techniques, and Models of Computer Programming
- Barendregt, The Lambda Calculus. it is true that the λ-cube is rarely useful within the tight confines of a knifefight. after a long day of bandanas and leather gloves and switchblades, even the brawler must eventually go home to family and fire and food and F systems. in a pinch, its bedazzling yellow cover can blind opponents.
speaking of math, you might want to take a look at Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right and Knuth's Concrete Mathematics. you'll want to know your combinatorics, your prob/stats, and your linear algebra cold. calculus through diffeqs is necessary to know, but i'm a pretty hardcore nerd and yet don't find myself integrating things all that often.
now go forth and fight in the streets. i list no machine learning because i dislike machine learning. there are no quantum books because quantum is not yet useful for streetfighting (we all look forward to this situation changing). i list no SIMT/accelerator books because they're all shite. i list no infosec because infosec is a subfield of QA, fight me. there are no links because i'm a lazy, lazy man.
i've heard good things about Tim Roughgarden's algorithms books, and have them on my shelves to read soon, but cannot yet speak to them. likewise Beej's book on networking, though that looks kinda lightweight. neither he nor Stevens goes into modern fast networking using things like XDP and Io_uring.
you should of course also read Hacking the Planet with Notcurses, buying copies for your team and family.

articles.title: Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation
articles.body:
Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation (fastcompany.com) 44
			
		 	
				October 3:  $84,680
Today:  $64,108
Bitcoin dropped 24.2% in 46 days.  And it "fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500," reports Fortune, "wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over."
The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm's demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again.   The recent downturn has also extended to other parts of the crypto market. That includes Tether's USDT, the largest cryptocurrency pegged to the U.S. dollar, whose total value shrank by $7.7 billion over the past two months, according to CryptoQuant, a sign that less cash is available in crypto markets.
This time around, inflation has been the main culprit. Tuesday's Consumer Price Index report showed prices rose 0.4% in October, more than economists expected. Even stripping out food and energy, inflation ran hotter than forecast. Traders now overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in December, with some betting on an even bigger increase.   "Because these are non-yielding assets, and we expect inflation to rise... people are chucking stuff like gold and Bitcoin to find... government bonds that are going up, providing you [with] income," Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at financial technology company IG Group, told Fortune...
Heavy borrowing and spending on AI have created what 21Shares calls an "AI black hole," drawing money toward the sector and away from assets like Bitcoin and gold. But Bitcoin remains "joined at the hip" with tech stocks, according to Beauchamp. That leaves it in an awkward position: It faces competition for investment dollars when enthusiasm for AI runs high, yet can get dragged down when that enthusiasm fades.  
Fast Company points out Bitcoin "remains down more than 20% since the beginning of 2026."
[Nvidia] has seen its shares lose more than 27% of their value over the past month.  The tech sell-off seems to have dragged down the crypto markets, too, as the two sectors are, on some levels, intermingled... On top of that, outflows from Bitcoin funds may also be contributing to the slide. More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were closed in recent days, which may have added to declining demand, affecting BTC prices.

articles.title: Disk encryption on NetBSD – achieving secrecy
articles.body:
Threat models
These are two threat models for which disk encryption is the answer:
- The device is stolen or lost and its contents must remain secret.
- The device is tampered with, and all attempts at tampering must render it unusable.
Right now, we will focus on the first threat model. It is very difficult to build a tamper-proof system, and you need to worry about tamper-proofing your hardware, depending on what kind of actor is a realistic threat.
If we want to keep data on the system secret, we must first consider which data is worth protecting. On a NetBSD system, our data can be grouped into two broad categories:
- System files (open source software)
- User-modified files
Does the /bin/sh executable downloaded from the NetBSD FTP server contain any sensitive information?
On a BSD system, due to the separation of the base system and packages, many root file system directories are mostly unmodified outside of upgrades. In a properly configured system, nearly all system daemons and user applications are not going to be running as root, so won’t have permission to modify or create files in /bin.
We can reasonably assume that /bin/sh is the same binary that every other NetBSD user is running. A user may even opt to make directories containing such system files read-only.
Problems with disk encryption
The operating system needs to be able to load files to boot.[citation needed] This makes "true" full disk encryption difficult to achieve without specialized hardware, since the user needs some way to enter a password or an encryption key, and can’t do so without some form of software running on their computer. NetBSD also needs to store some amount of metadata about the encrypted partition on the disk, such as information on how to generate a secure 256-bit key from a 24 character password.
It is common for Unix systems to use shared libraries, which are loaded by programs to access system functionality. If these become unavailable, for example, by /usr/lib going missing, it becomes much harder to use the system. Familiarize yourself with the standard utilities in /rescue which don’t need working shared libraries to be useful.
The cryptographic algorithms that get standardized by the US government tend to be slow when implemented in software. This carries a performance penalty. As a result, many modern CPUs include implementations of ciphers like AES in hardware. For those that don’t, there’s alternative ciphers like Adiantum.
Which directories are sensitive?
And which are necessary for the OS to load?
On a normal NetBSD system, several directories have a high chance of being modified during system operation:
- 
/home - user-specific files
- 
/var - log files, system-wide databases (e.g. mail notifications), crash dumps…
- 
/root - configuration files relevant to the root user account
- 
/usr/pkg and /usr/local - where third-party software is installed
- 
/etc - init scripts, system-wide configuration for the base system
A simple approach might be to encrypt /home. However, this might not be enough for some users. Although the crash directory can be easily changed with
sysctl,
a crash dump contains a snapshot of system memory which might be sensitive. If any servers have been run on the system, the log files might be sensitive. Mail sent to users (e.g. about their interrupted vi sessions and associated backups) might reveal sensitive file names.
Some users opt for the
cgdroot
approach, which uses only a small unencrypted ramdisk to pivot to an encrypted file system. However, this modifies the system startup routines significantly and may make certain rescue options harder. So, it’s worth asking whether there’s an approach that is somewhere in the middle, and still uses the standard NetBSD installation and boot process. Many BSD systems use separate file system partitions for /usr and /var, and this is a standard configuration supported by the NetBSD installer.
/etc is a harder problem to solve, since it contains files necessary to boot the system. However, on a typical desktop system, many files in /etc remain untouched. Passwords in /etc are generally stored only in hash form, except for Wi-Fi access points and certain VPN configurations (although it’s easy to reconfigure wpa_supplicant_flags to use a different configuration file from the default one in /etc). Many configuration files are only loaded much later in the boot process, after /usr is already mounted, and can easily be replaced with symbolic links to files on another file system.
The installation process
The NetBSD installer has basic functionality, but gets the job done quickly. In this configuration, we’re going to install NetBSD to a small unencrypted root file system. When you start to ignore the growth that can occur in /usr and /var and /home, even a complete NetBSD installation with development tools included is tiny. 4 GB should be more than enough.
For example purposes, I am going to use a sparc64 virtual machine, but the process is basically the same for more mainstream CPU architectures like amd64.
The installer detects that we already have a partitioned disk. We’re going to pick the "e: Delete everything" option so we have a fresh disk to start with:
Next, we’re going to choose "Set sizes of NetBSD partitions". This will allow us to have a small root, and reserve a large encrypted partition:
Here, I’ve decided I want a 4096 MB (4 GB) root file system, and a 11263 MB (11 GB) partition allocated for /var. Later, we’ll make /usr and /var share a disk partition, so don’t worry about this too much. Select "Go on".
On the next screen, I’ve changed the type of the secondary partition to "cgd" (listed under "Other type"), NetBSD’s encrypted device driver. I’ve also set its mount point to "-" so we can reconfigure it later:
I tell the installer I want to do a Full Installation and it completes as normal, installing everything into the small root partition.
When we reboot and log in as root, we enter a new world… our 4 GB unencrypted root partition.
Post-installation setup (disklabel)
Since I’m on sparc64, the disk is partitioned into disklabels. wd0 is the primary drive, and the disklabel command shows that /dev/wd0d is the partition reserved for our encrypted file system:
# disklabel wd0
#        size    offset     fstype [fsize bsize cpg/sgs]
 a:   8389584         0     4.2BSD      0     0     0  # (Cyl.      0 -   8322)
 b:   2097152   8389584       swap                     # (Cyl.   8323 -  10403*)
 c:  33554432         0     unused      0     0        # (Cyl.      0 -  33288*)
 d:  23067072  10487232        cgd                     # (Cyl.  10404 -  33287)
We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd:
# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/wd0d adiantum 256
And then load the configuration and set our password:
# cgdconfig -V re-enter cgd0 /dev/wd0d
Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.
The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.
This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another disklabel inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid disklabel, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.
# disklabel -i cgd0
This opens the interactive editor. We’re going to enter N to set a name for our disklabel (enter something like "cgdlabel"), then enter a to modify the first sub-partition.
First, it asks for a file system type. Enter ? to display a list of types:
partition>a
Filesystem type [unused]: ?
Supported file system types:
Since I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, I’m going to enter "4.4LFS". A more common and well-tested configuration would be "4.2BSD".
Next is the start offset and partition size:
Start offset ('x' to start after partition 'x') [0c, 0s, 0M]: 0
Partition size ('$' for all remaining) [0c, 0s, 0M]: $
Since "a" is the only sub-partition at the moment, the default start of 0 is fine. "$" will use all available space on the cgd.
Finally, we’ll save our new label and quit the disklabel editor:
partition>W
Label disk [n]?y
Label written
partition>Q
Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/wd0d to disklabel,
and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:
cgd0 /dev/wd0d /etc/cgd/wd0d
We can now access this hidden partition as /dev/cgd0a. But for it to be useful, we’ll need to create a file system on it. Once again, here I’m using the Log File System:
# newfs_lfs /dev/rcgd0a
A more normal and well-tested configuration would be FFSv2ea:
# newfs -O2ea /dev/rcgd0a
We can now mount and access the encrypted file system:
# mkdir -p /encfs
# mount /dev/cgd0a /encfs
Add a new line in /etc/fstab for our encrypted mount point:
/dev/cgd0a      /encfs  lfs     rw,noatime      1 2
Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.
Post-installation setup (disk wedges)
On a recent amd64 machine, your system probably uses GPT and disk wedges instead of disklabels. Assuming our primary disk is ld0, we can see a list of wedges with dkctl:
# dkctl ld0 listwedges
/dev/rld0: 3 wedges:
dk0: 20e57277-ad70-408e-9c68-225270ed1500, 9267072 blocks at 64, type: ffs
dk1: abad5a2d-8411-4d36-980e-a5f2b03a1047, 4194304 blocks at 9267136, type: swap
dk2: 2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661, 53647360 blocks at 13461440, type: cgd
In this case, our partition reserved for our encrypted file system is /dev/dk2, also accessible via the UUID alias NAME=2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661.
We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd:
# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/maincgd aes-cbc 256
And then load the configuration and set our password:
# cgdconfig -V re-enter cgd0 NAME=2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661 /etc/cgd/maincgd
Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.
The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.
This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another GPT partition table inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid GPT table, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.
# gpt create cgd0
Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/maincgd to gpt,
and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:

These are required regardless of whether using disklabel or wedges.

Then, we move our important directories out of the way and replace them with links to the encrypted ones:

# /rescue/ln -s /encfs/home /home
# /rescue/mv /var /var2
# /rescue/ln -s /encfs/var /var
# /rescue/mv /usr /usr2
# /rescue/ln -s /encfs/usr /usr

After this process, the NetBSD installer is not aware of the encrypted partition existing during upgrades. Online upgrades must be used, rather than offline upgrades where the installer is booted from removable media. This may be done with a tool like sysupgrade.

articles.title: Disk encryption on NetBSD – achieving secrecy
articles.body:
Threat models
These are two threat models for which disk encryption is the answer:
- The device is stolen or lost and its contents must remain secret.
- The device is tampered with, and all attempts at tampering must render it unusable.
Right now, we will focus on the first threat model. It is very difficult to build a tamper-proof system, and you need to worry about tamper-proofing your hardware, depending on what kind of actor is a realistic threat.
If we want to keep data on the system secret, we must first consider which data is worth protecting. On a NetBSD system, our data can be grouped into two broad categories:
- System files (open source software)
- User-modified files
Does the /bin/sh executable downloaded from the NetBSD FTP server contain any sensitive information?
On a BSD system, due to the separation of the base system and packages, many root file system directories are mostly unmodified outside of upgrades. In a properly configured system, nearly all system daemons and user applications are not going to be running as root, so won’t have permission to modify or create files in /bin.
We can reasonably assume that /bin/sh is the same binary that every other NetBSD user is running. A user may even opt to make directories containing such system files read-only.
Problems with disk encryption
The operating system needs to be able to load files to boot.[citation needed] This makes "true" full disk encryption difficult to achieve without specialized hardware, since the user needs some way to enter a password or an encryption key, and can’t do so without some form of software running on their computer. NetBSD also needs to store some amount of metadata about the encrypted partition on the disk, such as information on how to generate a secure 256-bit key from a 24 character password.
It is common for Unix systems to use shared libraries, which are loaded by programs to access system functionality. If these become unavailable, for example, by /usr/lib going missing, it becomes much harder to use the system. Familiarize yourself with the standard utilities in /rescue which don’t need working shared libraries to be useful.
The cryptographic algorithms that get standardized by the US government tend to be slow when implemented in software. This carries a performance penalty. As a result, many modern CPUs include implementations of ciphers like AES in hardware. For those that don’t, there’s alternative ciphers like Adiantum.
Which directories are sensitive?
And which are necessary for the OS to load?
On a normal NetBSD system, several directories have a high chance of being modified during system operation:
- 
/home - user-specific files
- 
/var - log files, system-wide databases (e.g. mail notifications), crash dumps…
- 
/root - configuration files relevant to the root user account
- 
/usr/pkg and /usr/local - where third-party software is installed
- 
/etc - init scripts, system-wide configuration for the base system
A simple approach might be to encrypt /home. However, this might not be enough for some users. Although the crash directory can be easily changed with
sysctl,
a crash dump contains a snapshot of system memory which might be sensitive. If any servers have been run on the system, the log files might be sensitive. Mail sent to users (e.g. about their interrupted vi sessions and associated backups) might reveal sensitive file names.
Some users opt for the
cgdroot
approach, which uses only a small unencrypted ramdisk to pivot to an encrypted file system. However, this modifies the system startup routines significantly and may make certain rescue options harder. So, it’s worth asking whether there’s an approach that is somewhere in the middle, and still uses the standard NetBSD installation and boot process. Many BSD systems use separate file system partitions for /usr and /var, and this is a standard configuration supported by the NetBSD installer.
/etc is a harder problem to solve, since it contains files necessary to boot the system. However, on a typical desktop system, many files in /etc remain untouched. Passwords in /etc are generally stored only in hash form, except for Wi-Fi access points and certain VPN configurations (although it’s easy to reconfigure wpa_supplicant_flags to use a different configuration file from the default one in /etc). Many configuration files are only loaded much later in the boot process, after /usr is already mounted, and can easily be replaced with symbolic links to files on another file system.
The installation process
The NetBSD installer has basic functionality, but gets the job done quickly. In this configuration, we’re going to install NetBSD to a small unencrypted root file system. When you start to ignore the growth that can occur in /usr and /var and /home, even a complete NetBSD installation with development tools included is tiny. 4 GB should be more than enough.
For example purposes, I am going to use a sparc64 virtual machine, but the process is basically the same for more mainstream CPU architectures like amd64.
The installer detects that we already have a partitioned disk. We’re going to pick the "e: Delete everything" option so we have a fresh disk to start with:
Next, we’re going to choose "Set sizes of NetBSD partitions". This will allow us to have a small root, and reserve a large encrypted partition:
Here, I’ve decided I want a 4096 MB (4 GB) root file system, and a 11263 MB (11 GB) partition allocated for /var. Later, we’ll make /usr and /var share a disk partition, so don’t worry about this too much. Select "Go on".
On the next screen, I’ve changed the type of the secondary partition to "cgd" (listed under "Other type"), NetBSD’s encrypted device driver. I’ve also set its mount point to "-" so we can reconfigure it later:
I tell the installer I want to do a Full Installation and it completes as normal, installing everything into the small root partition.
When we reboot and log in as root, we enter a new world… our 4 GB unencrypted root partition.
Post-installation setup (disklabel)
Since I’m on sparc64, the disk is partitioned into disklabels. wd0 is the primary drive, and the disklabel command shows that /dev/wd0d is the partition reserved for our encrypted file system:
# disklabel wd0
#        size    offset     fstype [fsize bsize cpg/sgs]
 a:   8389584         0     4.2BSD      0     0     0  # (Cyl.      0 -   8322)
 b:   2097152   8389584       swap                     # (Cyl.   8323 -  10403*)
 c:  33554432         0     unused      0     0        # (Cyl.      0 -  33288*)
 d:  23067072  10487232        cgd                     # (Cyl.  10404 -  33287)
We can go directly ahead with creating a parameters file for the cgd:
# cgdconfig -g -k argon2id -o /etc/cgd/wd0d adiantum 256
And then load the configuration and set our password:
# cgdconfig -V re-enter cgd0 /dev/wd0d
Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.
The next time we enter our password, we want to be able to verify that the password was correct, to avoid reading or writing invalid data.
This is done by choosing a verification method based on the contents of the encrypted partition. For flexibility’s sake, we’re going to put another disklabel inside the encrypted partition. This will allow the system to easily verify the password is correct by looking for a valid disklabel, but also gives us flexibility in our choice of file system.
# disklabel -i cgd0
This opens the interactive editor. We’re going to enter N to set a name for our disklabel (enter something like "cgdlabel"), then enter a to modify the first sub-partition.
First, it asks for a file system type. Enter ? to display a list of types:
partition>a
Filesystem type [unused]: ?
Supported file system types:
Since I’m running -current and want to test the Log File System, I’m going to enter "4.4LFS". A more common and well-tested configuration would be "4.2BSD".
Next is the start offset and partition size:
Start offset ('x' to start after partition 'x') [0c, 0s, 0M]: 0
Partition size ('$' for all remaining) [0c, 0s, 0M]: $
Since "a" is the only sub-partition at the moment, the default start of 0 is fine. "$" will use all available space on the cgd.
Finally, we’ll save our new label and quit the disklabel editor:
partition>W
Label disk [n]?y
Label written
partition>Q
Now change the verify_method in /etc/cgd/wd0d to disklabel,
and add a line in /etc/cgd/cgd.conf to create the cgd at boot time:
cgd0 /dev/wd0d /etc/cgd/wd0d
We can now access this hidden partition as /dev/cgd0a. But for it to be useful, we’ll need to create a file system on it. Once again, here I’m using the Log File System:
# newfs_lfs /dev/rcgd0a
A more normal and well-tested configuration would be FFSv2ea:
# newfs -O2ea /dev/rcgd0a
We can now mount and access the encrypted file system:
# mkdir -p /encfs
# mount /dev/cgd0a /encfs
Add a new line in /etc/fstab for our encrypted mount point:
/dev/cgd0a      /encfs  lfs     rw,noatime      1 2
Use "ffs" instead of "lfs" if you aren’t using the Log File System. If using FFS, you may want to use the options rw,log,noatime to enable journaling.
Post-installation setup (disk wedges)
On a recent amd64 machine, your system probably uses GPT and disk wedges instead of disklabels. Assuming our primary disk is ld0, we can see a list of wedges with dkctl:
# dkctl ld0 listwedges
/dev/rld0: 3 wedges:
dk0: 20e57277-ad70-408e-9c68-225270ed1500, 9267072 blocks at 64, type: ffs
dk1: abad5a2d-8411-4d36-980e-a5f2b03a1047, 4194304 blocks at 9267136, type: swap
dk2: 2c4d136a-f7ed-48f8-aae8-38afdd50c661, 53647360 blocks at 13461440, type: cgd

Now cgd0 appears to the system as yet another disk, but all attempts to access that disk will be automatically encrypted/decrypted by the kernel.

articles.title: Dartmouth (Guarini) will not admit math PhD cohort this year
articles.body:
The Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies has suspended admissions to the next cohort in its math Ph.D. program, which would matriculate in the 2027-2028 academic year. Guarini dean Carrie Colla ’01 and College spokesperson Jana Barnello did not specify when or whether the program would resume admissions.
Colla wrote in a Nov. 10 email statement to The Dartmouth that Guarini “regularly considers how to best invest in graduate education.”
“As part of those regular reviews, we are pausing admissions to the math Ph.D. program for the 2027-2028 cycle while the School of Arts and Sciences conducts a department review,” she wrote.
The decision to suspend the program “was made in close partnership with leaders in the School of Arts and Sciences and we look forward to working collaboratively with the department on this review,” Colla added.
She wrote in a Nov. 10 email to current graduate students that there “will be opportunities for students to participate in the review” and that she would meet with math graduate students and department faculty on Nov. 17. Graduate students can also reach out to math department chair Dimitrios Giannakis and math professor Vladimir Chernov to share questions and concerns, she wrote.
“While I know it is disappointing news that your cohort will not be growing next year, I am confident that this approach will allow us to strengthen the experience of both our Ph.D. students and the undergraduate students in the department,” Colla wrote.
During a Q&A at the Nov. 9 general faculty meeting, which The Dartmouth attended but was not permitted to record, faculty raised concerns about the suspension. Math professor Peter Winkler, who opposed the suspension, said at the meeting the decision was communicated to math department faculty on Nov. 6. Winkler declined to provide additional comment after the meeting.
The Ph.D. program’s pause follows a national trend of decreasing Ph.D. program seats. Data collected from 55 undisclosed research institutions demonstrated that Ph.D. acceptances dropped 15% in 2026 from the previous year, even though domestic applications increased.
In a Nov. 10 email to current graduate students, which was obtained and reviewed by The Dartmouth, Giannakis wrote that faculty members were “continuing to engage” with College administrators to “find a path forward” that would “eventually resume” the Ph.D. program.
Giannakis added in the email that Colla and School of Arts and Sciences dean Nina Pavcnik would attend a math department faculty meeting on Nov. 11 to discuss the suspension. 
“While I do not expect a reversal of the decision to pause admissions, I hope there will at least be a constructive dialogue with actionable outcomes,” he wrote. 
Giannakis was unable to comment by time of publication.
The Guarini admissions office communicated the decision to applicants on Nov. 10, according to an email obtained by The Dartmouth. Any materials or recommendation letters that have already been submitted “will not be reviewed,” the Guarini admissions office wrote. Applications for the program, which typically accepts seven to nine students per year, would have been due on Dec. 15, 2026, according to the math department website.
“We recognize this is disappointing news and we are sorry for the disruption to your plans,” the email to people who already submitted application materials reads. 
On Nov. 10, Colla wrote to current math graduate students that “status and support” for current students “are not changing” and that the program will see “every currently enrolled student through graduation,” according to an email obtained and reviewed by The Dartmouth.
“Stipends, insurance and the five-year funding guarantee all remain in place for students making satisfactory academic progress,” Colla wrote. “Advising relationships, qualifying exams, degree requirements and teaching and research appointments will continue as planned.”
Guarini Ph.D. students received an annual stipend of $49,862.40 for the 2026-2027 academic year, along with tuition remission, health insurance and other benefits, according to the Guarini website. The College guarantees five years of financial support to students making satisfactory academic progress.
Graduate students typically teach “one course in each of their final three years of study,” according to the math department graduate student handbook. Starting this term, math Ph.D. candidates must also serve as a teaching assistant for one term each year after their third year, while first and second-year Ph.D. candidates must serve as teaching assistants for three terms a year instead of the previously required two, according to the handbook.
Third-year math Ph.D. candidate Jacob Lehmann Duke GR said he and his fellow graduate students learned of the suspension from Colla’s Nov. 10 email. He said he was “frustrated” by the “lack of transparency” surrounding the decision. 
“We were all shocked,” he said. “There was no indication that this was coming.”
Second-year math Ph.D. candidate Alex Moon GR said they believe suspending applications for the upcoming cycle sends “a message of instability” to future applicants.
“Part of the deal of graduate school is that you want there to be minimal factors outside of your control that will prevent you from getting this Ph.D.,” Moon said. “If this is something they do once, it’s something they can do later.”
In an interview with The Dartmouth, second-year math Ph.D. candidate Aidan Hennessey GR said “losing out on a cohort of students” would negatively affect the discussions among the “already quite small” Ph.D. program.
“Having people in adjacent areas of math to you — that you can talk about math and learn from, teach and talk through ideas with — all of this is very helpful,” Hennessey said. “Having more students around is nice for community.”
Lehmann Duke added that the suspension could put undergraduates intending to enroll in graduate-level mathematics courses “at a real deficit.”
Ben Singer ’27 — who said they have taken graduate-level math courses since their freshman year — added that there are “a few core graduate courses” that are “really important for undergraduates here who want to get into graduate school.” A decrease in Ph.D. students raises questions about whether those classes will be offered, whether undergraduates will be able to take them and how fewer course offerings will affect people who want to go to graduate school, Singer said.
The College “reserves the right to make changes in the offering” or cancel a course with fewer than five enrolled students, according to the Arts and Sciences Registrar’s Office website.
First-year computational science and modeling Ph.D. candidate Ethan Baird GR said “almost half” of his program’s coursework requirements are typically fulfilled through mathematics department courses. Baird added that these classes are the “basis of everything that we end up doing later,” which leads him to worry that the suspension of the admissions will have trickle-down effects on the computational science and modeling Ph.D. programs. 
Math major Ribhu Hooja ’27 said the department “did not officially” inform undergraduate students about the pause and that he instead found out from graduate students. If the pause lasts “even for a year, there could still be harm” because of “the relationships formed” between undergraduate and graduate students in advanced math classes, Hooja said.
“We learn how to apply to grad school, and what it means,” Hooja said. “It’s an important relationship I’ve really benefitted a lot from.”
Third-year Ph.D. candidate Michaela Polley GR said she was concerned about the pause’s effects on “research culture” among Dartmouth graduates and undergraduates alike.
“The idea of being a research university and a liberal arts college doesn’t work if you don’t have graduate students,” she said.
During the Nov. 9 meeting, College President Sian Leah Beilock and Pavcnik also addressed faculty concerns about the College’s discontinuation of the Society of Fellows, a three-year interdisciplinary research program established in 2014 to support postdoctoral research and scholarship. The Society has stopped recruiting new fellows and will conclude in summer 2028, when its current cohort completes their appointments, according to the program’s website. 
Beilock said at the meeting that the decision follows the need to reinvest funding in other institutional priorities.
Beilock announced at the meeting that the College is “working to reduce Dartmouth’s spending by $50 million,” in order to increase faculty and staff salaries “especially if and when inflation continues to rise,” according to a transcript of her speech published on the Office of the President’s website.
In a Nov. 11 email statement to The Dartmouth, Barnello wrote that the $50 million “reflects adjustments already made” to the budget, and that “roughly half” is “already in place” for fiscal year 2027.
Beilock also announced at the meeting that the College is “preparing” to convert North Park apartments, which are currently listed on the Office of Residential Life website as undergraduate housing, to graduate student housing. The North Park apartments have exclusively housed undergraduates since the 2022-2023 academic year, according to the Dartmouth Graduate Student Council website.
Correction appended (Nov. 12, 9:30 a.m.): A previous version of this article referred to Alex Moon as he. They use they/them pronouns.
Sahil Gandhi ’29 is a reporter from Staten Island, N.Y., and is majoring in environmental studies and government modified with philosophy and economics. He loves word searches and falling down internet and Wikipedia rabbit holes. He can be reached at sgandhi@thedartmouth.com.
