First-year computational science and modeling Ph.D. candidate Ethan Baird GR said “almost half” of his program’s coursework requirements are typically fulfilled through mathematics department courses. Baird added that these classes are the “basis of everything that we end up doing later,” which leads him to worry that the suspension of the admissions will have trickle-down effects on the computational science and modeling Ph.D. programs. 
Math major Ribhu Hooja ’27 said the department “did not officially” inform undergraduate students about the pause and that he instead found out from graduate students. If the pause lasts “even for a year, there could still be harm” because of “the relationships formed” between undergraduate and graduate students in advanced math classes, Hooja said.
“We learn how to apply to grad school, and what it means,” Hooja said. “It’s an important relationship I’ve really benefitted a lot from.”
Third-year Ph.D. candidate Michaela Polley GR said she was concerned about the pause’s effects on “research culture” among Dartmouth graduates and undergraduates alike.
“The idea of being a research university and a liberal arts college doesn’t work if you don’t have graduate students,” she said.
During the Nov. 9 meeting, College President Sian Leah Beilock and Pavcnik also addressed faculty concerns about the College’s discontinuation of the Society of Fellows, a three-year interdisciplinary research program established in 2014 to support postdoctoral research and scholarship. The Society has stopped recruiting new fellows and will conclude in summer 2028, when its current cohort completes their appointments, according to the program’s website. 
Beilock said at the meeting that the decision follows the need to reinvest funding in other institutional priorities.
Beilock announced at the meeting that the College is “working to reduce Dartmouth’s spending by $50 million,” in order to increase faculty and staff salaries “especially if and when inflation continues to rise,” according to a transcript of her speech published on the Office of the President’s website.
In a Nov. 11 email statement to The Dartmouth, Barnello wrote that the $50 million “reflects adjustments already made” to the budget, and that “roughly half” is “already in place” for fiscal year 2027.
Beilock also announced at the meeting that the College is “preparing” to convert North Park apartments, which are currently listed on the Office of Residential Life website as undergraduate housing, to graduate student housing. The North Park apartments have exclusively housed undergraduates since the 2022-2023 academic year, according to the Dartmouth Graduate Student Council website.
Correction appended (Nov. 12, 9:30 a.m.): A previous version of this article referred to Alex Moon as he. They use they/them pronouns.
Sahil Gandhi ’29 is a reporter from Staten Island, N.Y., and is majoring in environmental studies and government modified with philosophy and economics. He loves word searches and falling down internet and Wikipedia rabbit holes. He can be reached at sgandhi@thedartmouth.com.

articles.title: Creating a self booting ZIP archive
articles.body:
So, after a debugging session the other day, I was having some shower thoughts regarding early userspace and initrd.
Linux initramfs supports unpacking CPIO, a stupid, simple, standardized format. In the discussion on whether to support TAR instead, much emphasize has been put on the fact that CPIO is standardized and less fragmented.
Luckily, Linux (the kernel) includes its own tool to produce the specific variant of the standard that it happens to implement. The standard CPIO tool is possibly the most cursed archiver under the SUN.
In the old DOS/WinDOS world, ZIP was probably the most wide spread and well known archive format, being displaced to some extend by the rise of RAR during the 2000s.
Because of the design of the format, ZIP lends itself to all kinds of polyglot trickery. Way back when, self extracting ZIP archives where a thing, EXE/ZIP polyglots that can be run and unpack themselves, which is useful if you don't have an archiver installed.
I don't think I need to explain where I am going with this, here is the resulting ZIP archive I built:
Download boot.zip
It is a completely normal ZIP archive, containing its own source code needed to build itself from scratch:
$ unzip -t boot.zip
Archive:  boot.zip
    testing: boot/ZIPHEAD.COM         OK
    testing: boot/MESSAGE.TXT         OK
    testing: common/asm.h             OK
    testing: common/multiboot.h       OK
    testing: common/zip.h             OK
    testing: multiboot/console.c      OK
    testing: multiboot/console.h      OK
    testing: multiboot/multiboot.c    OK
    testing: multiboot/string.S       OK
    testing: setup/a20.S              OK
    testing: setup/disk.S             OK
    testing: setup/entry16.S          OK
    testing: setup/entry32.S          OK
    testing: setup/mbload.S           OK
    testing: setup/mem.S              OK
    testing: setup/setup.ld           OK
    testing: util/fixhdr.c            OK
    testing: util/zipglue.c           OK
    testing: util/zippack.c           OK
    testing: mk.sh                    OK
    testing: README.txt               OK
    testing: MESSAGE.txt              OK
    testing: LICENSE.txt              OK
No errors detected in compressed data of boot.zip.
    A particularly interesting file here is boot/ZIPHEAD.COM, that contains executable code that is run when booting the archive.
You need to fix the execute permissions of mk.sh after unpacking, and you will need a copy of Zlib installed for the tools. Running mk.sh from it's directory should leave you with a fresh copy of the bootable ZIP archive.
The simplest way to run it, is to just pass it to Qemu direct kernel boot:
$ qemu-system-i386 -kernel boot.zip
"That's easy" you might say, "Qemu supports Multiboot, that ZIPHEAD.COM is uncompressed, at the beginning of the archive and has a Multiboot header in it!"
Yes, that's all true! But this ZIP archive also brings it's own boot loader along. You can try putting it on a floppy and throw that in front of Qemu:
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=floppy.img count=2880
$ dd if=boot.zip of=floppy.img conv=notrunc
$ qemu-system-i386 -fda floppy.img
The first 512 bytes of the archive contain a valid boot sector that loads some more code from the second sector and then bootstraps itself into highmem with the A20 enabled and 32 bit protected mode set up.
You can also put it on a hard drive too, it detects what INT 13h drive it's been loaded from and dutifully queries the disk geometry.
If you care to try, you can also dump it on a real floppy and stuff it into a PC:
That's a Pentium MMX by the way, but I also tried an i486 DX2 and an Am386DX-40, just to be sure. My 486 had me hold my breath for a moment, it has a spectacularly slow floppy drive. The text on screen is from the file boot/MESSAGE.TXT
"But that's not special either" you might respond, "ZIPs are read from the back, you can just put anything you want in front, so you put a boot sector there!"
That is sadly not quite true anymore, I'll get to that. But for now, lets take a look at the first couple bytes of that archive together and we'll see the real party trick:
$ xxd -g 1 -l 128 boot.zip
00000000: 50 4b 03 04 0a 00 02 80 00 00 eb 44 e4 2e 41 0f  PK.........D..A.
00000010: 01 8f 0a 09 00 00 0a 09 00 00 10 00 00 00 62 6f  ..............bo
00000020: 6f 74 2f 5a 49 50 48 45 41 44 2e 43 4f 4d 00 90  ot/ZIPHEAD.COM..
00000030: 02 b0 ad 1b 03 00 01 00 fb 4f 51 e4 30 00 10 00  .........OQ.0...
00000040: 00 00 10 00 bd 72 10 00 bd 72 10 00 31 03 10 00  .....r...r..1...
00000050: fa fc 31 c0 89 c4 8e d8 8e c0 8e d0 ea 61 7c 00  ..1..........a|.
00000060: 00 bf 00 06 b9 00 02 f3 aa 88 16 98 06 be 0f 7d  ...............}
00000070: e8 8c 00 b8 00 f0 89 c1 50 9d 9c 58 a8 02 74 4a  ........P..X..tJ
The ASCII P stands for Phil ( not Picard ), as in Phil Katz, followed by 03h and 04h. What you are looking at, is a completely valid ZIP local file header for boot/ZIPHEAD.COM
Oh, and those other bytes there after the ZIP header: 02 b0 ad 1b, if you flip them around to human endian, it reads 1BADB002. That's the Multiboot magic :-)
The 16 bit real mode code starts right after the Multiboot header, at offset 00000050. If you are feeling a little confused, so is the file utility:
$ file boot.zip
boot.zip: DOS/MBR boot sector; partition 1 : ID=0xd, active 0xcd, start-CHS (0x7
2,19,7), end-CHS (0x388,254,6), startsector 2147916342, 243810273 sectors; parti
tion 2 : ID=0x60, active 0x9c, start-CHS (0x366,6,3), end-CHS (0x3f7,49,18), sta
rtsector 2298911798, 4154016209 sectors; partition 4 : ID=0xf8, active 0xe1, sta
rt-CHS (0x2,184,1), end-CHS (0x313,6,13), startsector 3277940231, 0 sectors
If you take a closer look at the first line of the hex dump, you might be able to spot the jump instruction that makes this little magic trick possible. Luckily, Phil Katz' initials are valid opcodes. The Multiboot entry point is much further into the file at offset 00000331.
Here's a picture you probably recognize from the Wikipedia article about the ZIP format . This here is a local copy, Wikimedia Commons hosts the original with attribution and licensing information .
Much like a TAR or CPIO archive, a ZIP file is an amalgamation of tightly packed files with a short header in front, specifying the full file path and other meta data:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	uint16_t moddate;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t compsize;
	uint32_t origsize;
	uint16_t namelength;
	uint16_t extralength;
	char name[namelength];
	uint8_t extra[extralength];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_entry_t;
The timestamps are DOS datetime, the checksum is a CRC-32, there are no attributes or permission bits, we are thoroughly in DOS land. Directories are implied by the file paths.
Unlike TAR or CPIO, there is a central directory in the end, with a listing of all of the file headers and back references to the file in the archive. Unlike traditional file formats that have are started by a header, ZIP is terminated by a footer.
The reason for this is twofold:
That last part was especially important in the days when ZIP archives would be split over several floppies. To access a file, just scan the directory on the last floppy, then tell the user what floppy to insert to get the file.
By comparison, accessing a file in a tarball requires linearly scanning over the whole thing (which, on the other hand, is preferable for tape drives , where TAR originates).
ZIP archives are meant to be read from the back, the footer points to the central directory, the directory points to the files. In theory, the archiver shouldn't care if there happens to be a gap between two files, containing something else or if there is something else in the front of the archive, like a file header for a different file format.
The local file headers also supports up to 64k of "extra" stuff between the header and the file data, the footer has "comment" at the end, also up to 64k.
If you look at the footer for a second, you might spot an interesting design flaw:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t disknum;
	uint16_t diskstart;
	uint16_t num_dir_entries;
	uint16_t total_dir_entries;
	uint32_t dir_size;
	uint32_t dir_start;
	uint16_t comment_length;
	uint8_t comment[comment_length];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_end_t;
it is variable size, an archiver needs to find it looking from the back, but the magic and the size are both stored before the variable sized comment field. Ask yourself this for a moment: how would you implement this in an archiver? Demanding that there is no comment? Reading the last 64k plus some change and scanning it? From which direction? What if there is another valid footer inside the comment field of the footer? Depending on how an implementation deals with this, a specifically crafted archive can appear to contain different files when viewed with different archivers.
Trying to make the format extensible ended up building a whole lot of foot guns in there. And we are not even talking about the plethora of extensions that have been tacked on to the official specification over the years.
Many modern implementations decided to save themselves a lot of headaches and just treat ZIP archives the same way as tarballs, linearly scanning them from the front instead. They expect the archive to start with a local header, skipping by the size MUST lead to the next entry or finally, the central directory. They reject any archives where this is not possible. This effectively prevents a lot of polyglot trick fuckery, but at the cost of rendering possibly valid archives unreadable.
For the self booting ZIP archive, the challenge thus becomes: the archive MUST start with a local file header, there cannot be any gaps, everything must be properly contained inside files.
Anybody who has ever looked at a DIY toy OS tutorial has probably stumbled across The Multiboot Specification , the possibly easiest and most beginner friendly way to get a program running on bare metal x86.
The multiboot spec originates in the GNU/FSF ecosystem and is implemented by boot loaders like GRUB or Qemu direct kernel boot. SYSLINUX supports it via a plugin. There is a draft for an over engineered 2nd version, that also supports MIPS, but this is of no concert to us here.
A Multiboot 1 compliant kernel simply contains the magic value 0x1BADB002 somewhere in the first in the first 8k. This is followed by flags and a checksum (all 3 must add up to zero). Depending on the flags, additional fields may follow.
The kernel itself can be an ELF file from which the loader extracts load address and entry point. The kernel is run in 32 bit protected mode with flat segments (base=0, limit=4G) and the A20 gate enabled.
Alternatively to a plain old ELF file, the kernel can also specify the memory layout manually (indicated via a flag), allowing flat binaries or other file formats to be loaded. The extended header looks like this:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint32_t flags;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t hdr_addr;
	uint32_t load_addr;
	uint32_t load_end_addr;
	uint32_t bss_end_addr;
	uint32_t entry_point;
} mb_header_t;
The hdr_addr specifies the in-memory address of the header after loading the file, using this and the file offset where the header was found, the other addresses can be converted back to file offsets by the loader.
This way, the load_addr and load_end_addr are used to figure out what parts of the file to load where into memory. If the bss_end_addr is past that, the loader zero-fills it, before finally jumping to entry_point to run the kernel.
The Multiboot compliant loader also sets up a structure with system information (e.g. memory map, APM tables), kernel command line, etc… and passes the pointer to the kernel (via register EBX, magic value 0x2BADB002 in EAX).
Making a Multiboot bootable ZIP archive is trivial. Simply pack a flat binary with a Multiboot header as uncompressed file binary, make sure it is at the beginning and the addresses line up. An external tool can then fix up the headers, so that the whole archive is loaded.
For any practical applications, it would make sense to stop right here, but we're not here for "practical" or "sane".
On an IBM compatible machine, the BIOS iterates over the installed drives, loads the first sector from each (to location 0x7c00), until it finds one where the first sector ends with 0xaa55. It then jumps to the first byte.
Disks that are formatted with a filesystem, typically have a header in the beginning that starts with a jump instruction across the header into the bootstrap code that follows. The DOS MBR format opts to instead store the partition table at the end of the first sector and all the code in the front.
If we stuff a BIOS boot signature into the ZIP archive, at least parts of the ZIP local file header will be executed, the first few bytes are a mandated magic value and we cannot just put a jump instruction there.
The puzzle exercise now becomes, filling the header fields with values that make sense but also happen to be valid 8086 opcodes. At least, until we hit something that can be abused as a free-form field that we can stuff a jump into.
Let's take a look at that hex dump again:
I've tried to highlight the relevant header up to the jump instruction: 0xeb is a relative jump with a single byte immediate argument.
If we take a look again at the header structure, we can make out what fields those bytes correspond to:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	………
The timestamp is the first best place where we can put a jump instruction. The 0xeb relative jump works out to 8:30-ish in the morning, give or take the jump distance.
The two bytes in front of the modtime are compression method. We really, really want to have 0x0000 here, i.e. uncompressed, so that an archiver doesn't choke on the file data.
The first four bytes are the magic value of the format, we don't have any choice what to put here either, it has to be "PK\03\04". The version and flags fields are the only places where we have some creative freedom.
If we run the file through a dissassembler and take a look at the first few bytes, we'll end up with this:
$ objdump -D -m i8086 -b binary ./boot.zip
./boot.zip:     file format binary
Disassembly of section .data:
00000000 <.data>:
       0:       50                      push   %ax
       1:       4b                      dec    %bx
       2:       03 04                   add    (%si),%ax
       4:       0a 00                   or     (%bx,%si),%al
       6:       02 80 00 00             add    0x0(%bx,%si),%al
       a:       eb 44                   jmp    0x50
    This is AT&T syntax, source operands are left, destination on the right. We use GNU tools in this household, deal with it.
Anything that just fiddles around with a register doesn't really hurt us. Same goes for memory reads. We don't have memory protection, no matter what we access, there won't be any faults, the only memory mapped hardware around should be the frame buffer.
Memory writes are another story. Worst case, we could shoot up the interrupt vectors, the BIOS RAM areas (BDA, EBDA), or shadowed option ROMs.
The P for Phil also happens to also decode to push %ax. If the BIOS leaves us with a somewhat sane stack pointer, the push instruction should hopefully not mess anything up. It is part of the ZIP magic and thus unavoidable.
The version field is itself actually structured, containing a decimal encoded version number, followed by an OS ID byte. If we set it to 0x000a (stored as little endian), this decodes to version 1.0 on MS DOS.
0x0a is an orb, version 1.1 would be double byte sized, version 0.8 and 0.9 would be register direct and not touch the memory. An address of BX + SI is the result of a mod-reg-r/m field with all zeros.
We could try to code golf our way into consuming at least part of the flags as well, but low-valued, "harmless" opcodes that result in sane versions are sparse. Also, some version numbers change the meaning how an archiver is supposed to interpret the file. Also also, mod-reg-r/m combinations in the OS code field quickly end up as an undefined OS ID. Also also also, we have the method as well, that has to be 0x0000, which would result in a memory write if executed. We have to consume that somehow, rather than running it.
So for the flags, I came up with 0x8002 (stored as little endian). The lowest, set bit has a compression method dependent meaning, currently only defined for LZMA (14), deflate (8) and implode (6). For uncompressed (method 0) there is no defined meaning (the specification just ignores that part, it doesn't use nasty words like undefined). For deflate it would mean that maximum compression was used.
The MSB is specified as "reserved for use by PKWARE", whatever they chose to put there, if they ever chose anything at all. Most imporanly, the opcode 0x02 decodes to a single byte, indirect add, and in the mod-reg-r/m, the MSB tells the CPU to consume another 2 bytes of immediate DISPlacement. This is how we can get rid of the compression method.
At this point, we've made it! We reached the modtime field that we can just stuff a jump into.
Once we've made it past the header, we are in 16 bit real mode. We just need to go through all of the neccessary steps to set up the environment that the Multiboot code expects:
This might sound like a lot, but in the current version, the actual code boils down to 817 bytes. That includes all the headers (ZIP, multiboot), the rather bulky GDT. But it is still quite a lot and outside the scope of this post anyway, I might pick some interesting parts out of it for some follow-up posts (watch this space?).
The Multiboot entry code re-loads the GDT, but this time using the highmem location, and sets up a stack after the archive. The size is extracted from the Multiboot header. Knowing the start address, the C code can then iterate over itself to locate and access files in the archive.
Some linker script trickery is used to tie it all into one blob, but with the GDT and Multiboot header visible from both lomem and highmem code at different locations.
At this point, you might be inclined to actually read the source code in the ZIP archive. There are lots of comments trying to explain what is going on.
There's a README that points out the structure of the code with suggestions where to start reading. I decided to keep it readable rather than stuff it all into a single sector. Self-modifying trickery is kept to a minimum (to safe some space, the function to enter unreal mode modifies itself, the code is run twice, courtesy of a misdirected ret, entering protected mode the first time round, leaving it again and restoring the segment registers on the second run, before returning for real).
Code in the archive and this blog posts have been written with assistance from:
If you poke around in the code and have any suggestions for improvements, or otherwise do anything interesting with it, please let me know.
Have fun!

Unlike TAR or CPIO, there is a central directory in the end, with a listing of all of the file headers and back references to the file in the archive. Unlike traditional file formats that have are started by a header, ZIP is terminated by a footer.
The reason for this is twofold:
That last part was especially important in the days when ZIP archives would be split over several floppies. To access a file, just scan the directory on the last floppy, then tell the user what floppy to insert to get the file.
By comparison, accessing a file in a tarball requires linearly scanning over the whole thing (which, on the other hand, is preferable for tape drives , where TAR originates).
ZIP archives are meant to be read from the back, the footer points to the central directory, the directory points to the files. In theory, the archiver shouldn't care if there happens to be a gap between two files, containing something else or if there is something else in the front of the archive, like a file header for a different file format.
The local file headers also supports up to 64k of "extra" stuff between the header and the file data, the footer has "comment" at the end, also up to 64k.
If you look at the footer for a second, you might spot an interesting design flaw:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t disknum;
	uint16_t diskstart;
	uint16_t num_dir_entries;
	uint16_t total_dir_entries;
	uint32_t dir_size;
	uint32_t dir_start;
	uint16_t comment_length;
	uint8_t comment[comment_length];
} __attribute__((packed)) zip_end_t;
it is variable size, an archiver needs to find it looking from the back, but the magic and the size are both stored before the variable sized comment field. Ask yourself this for a moment: how would you implement this in an archiver? Demanding that there is no comment? Reading the last 64k plus some change and scanning it? From which direction? What if there is another valid footer inside the comment field of the footer? Depending on how an implementation deals with this, a specifically crafted archive can appear to contain different files when viewed with different archivers.
Trying to make the format extensible ended up building a whole lot of foot guns in there. And we are not even talking about the plethora of extensions that have been tacked on to the official specification over the years.
Many modern implementations decided to save themselves a lot of headaches and just treat ZIP archives the same way as tarballs, linearly scanning them from the front instead. They expect the archive to start with a local header, skipping by the size MUST lead to the next entry or finally, the central directory. They reject any archives where this is not possible. This effectively prevents a lot of polyglot trick fuckery, but at the cost of rendering possibly valid archives unreadable.
For the self booting ZIP archive, the challenge thus becomes: the archive MUST start with a local file header, there cannot be any gaps, everything must be properly contained inside files.
Anybody who has ever looked at a DIY toy OS tutorial has probably stumbled across The Multiboot Specification , the possibly easiest and most beginner friendly way to get a program running on bare metal x86.
The multiboot spec originates in the GNU/FSF ecosystem and is implemented by boot loaders like GRUB or Qemu direct kernel boot. SYSLINUX supports it via a plugin. There is a draft for an over engineered 2nd version, that also supports MIPS, but this is of no concert to us here.
A Multiboot 1 compliant kernel simply contains the magic value 0x1BADB002 somewhere in the first in the first 8k. This is followed by flags and a checksum (all 3 must add up to zero). Depending on the flags, additional fields may follow.
The kernel itself can be an ELF file from which the loader extracts load address and entry point. The kernel is run in 32 bit protected mode with flat segments (base=0, limit=4G) and the A20 gate enabled.
Alternatively to a plain old ELF file, the kernel can also specify the memory layout manually (indicated via a flag), allowing flat binaries or other file formats to be loaded. The extended header looks like this:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint32_t flags;
	uint32_t checksum;
	uint32_t hdr_addr;
	uint32_t load_addr;
	uint32_t load_end_addr;
	uint32_t bss_end_addr;
	uint32_t entry_point;
} mb_header_t;
The hdr_addr specifies the in-memory address of the header after loading the file, using this and the file offset where the header was found, the other addresses can be converted back to file offsets by the loader.
This way, the load_addr and load_end_addr are used to figure out what parts of the file to load where into memory. If the bss_end_addr is past that, the loader zero-fills it, before finally jumping to entry_point to run the kernel.
The Multiboot compliant loader also sets up a structure with system information (e.g. memory map, APM tables), kernel command line, etc… and passes the pointer to the kernel (via register EBX, magic value 0x2BADB002 in EAX).
Making a Multiboot bootable ZIP archive is trivial. Simply pack a flat binary with a Multiboot header as uncompressed file binary, make sure it is at the beginning and the addresses line up. An external tool can then fix up the headers, so that the whole archive is loaded.
For any practical applications, it would make sense to stop right here, but we're not here for "practical" or "sane".
On an IBM compatible machine, the BIOS iterates over the installed drives, loads the first sector from each (to location 0x7c00), until it finds one where the first sector ends with 0xaa55. It then jumps to the first byte.
Disks that are formatted with a filesystem, typically have a header in the beginning that starts with a jump instruction across the header into the bootstrap code that follows. The DOS MBR format opts to instead store the partition table at the end of the first sector and all the code in the front.
If we stuff a BIOS boot signature into the ZIP archive, at least parts of the ZIP local file header will be executed, the first few bytes are a mandated magic value and we cannot just put a jump instruction there.
The puzzle exercise now becomes, filling the header fields with values that make sense but also happen to be valid 8086 opcodes. At least, until we hit something that can be abused as a free-form field that we can stuff a jump into.
Let's take a look at that hex dump again:
I've tried to highlight the relevant header up to the jump instruction: 0xeb is a relative jump with a single byte immediate argument.
If we take a look again at the header structure, we can make out what fields those bytes correspond to:
typedef struct {
	uint32_t magic;
	uint16_t version;
	uint16_t flags;
	uint16_t method;
	uint16_t modtime;
	………
The timestamp is the first best place where we can put a jump instruction. The 0xeb relative jump works out to 8:30-ish in the morning, give or take the jump distance.
The two bytes in front of the modtime are compression method. We really, really want to have 0x0000 here, i.e. uncompressed, so that an archiver doesn't choke on the file data.
The first four bytes are the magic value of the format, we don't have any choice what to put here either, it has to be "PK\03\04". The version and flags fields are the only places where we have some creative freedom.
If we run the file through a dissassembler and take a look at the first few bytes, we'll end up with this:
$ objdump -D -m i8086 -b binary ./boot.zip
./boot.zip:     file format binary
Disassembly of section .data:
00000000 <.data>:
       0:       50                      push   %ax
       1:       4b                      dec    %bx
       2:       03 04                   add    (%si),%ax
       4:       0a 00                   or     (%bx,%si),%al
       6:       02 80 00 00             add    0x0(%bx,%si),%al
       a:       eb 44                   jmp    0x50
    This is AT&T syntax, source operands are left, destination on the right. We use GNU tools in this household, deal with it.
Anything that just fiddles around with a register doesn't really hurt us. Same goes for memory reads. We don't have memory protection, no matter what we access, there won't be any faults, the only memory mapped hardware around should be the frame buffer.
Memory writes are another story. Worst case, we could shoot up the interrupt vectors, the BIOS RAM areas (BDA, EBDA), or shadowed option ROMs.
The P for Phil also happens to also decode to push %ax. If the BIOS leaves us with a somewhat sane stack pointer, the push instruction should hopefully not mess anything up. It is part of the ZIP magic and thus unavoidable.
The version field is itself actually structured, containing a decimal encoded version number, followed by an OS ID byte. If we set it to 0x000a (stored as little endian), this decodes to version 1.0 on MS DOS.
0x0a is an orb, version 1.1 would be double byte sized, version 0.8 and 0.9 would be register direct and not touch the memory. An address of BX + SI is the result of a mod-reg-r/m field with all zeros.
We could try to code golf our way into consuming at least part of the flags as well, but low-valued, "harmless" opcodes that result in sane versions are sparse. Also, some version numbers change the meaning how an archiver is supposed to interpret the file. Also also, mod-reg-r/m combinations in the OS code field quickly end up as an undefined OS ID. Also also also, we have the method as well, that has to be 0x0000, which would result in a memory write if executed. We have to consume that somehow, rather than running it.
So for the flags, I came up with 0x8002 (stored as little endian). The lowest, set bit has a compression method dependent meaning, currently only defined for LZMA (14), deflate (8) and implode (6). For uncompressed (method 0) there is no defined meaning (the specification just ignores that part, it doesn't use nasty words like undefined). For deflate it would mean that maximum compression was used.
The MSB is specified as "reserved for use by PKWARE", whatever they chose to put there, if they ever chose anything at all. Most imporanly, the opcode 0x02 decodes to a single byte, indirect add, and in the mod-reg-r/m, the MSB tells the CPU to consume another 2 bytes of immediate DISPlacement. This is how we can get rid of the compression method.
At this point, we've made it! We reached the modtime field that we can just stuff a jump into.
Once we've made it past the header, we are in 16 bit real mode. We just need to go through all of the neccessary steps to set up the environment that the Multiboot code expects:
This might sound like a lot, but in the current version, the actual code boils down to 817 bytes. That includes all the headers (ZIP, multiboot), the rather bulky GDT. But it is still quite a lot and outside the scope of this post anyway, I might pick some interesting parts out of it for some follow-up posts (watch this space?).
The Multiboot entry code re-loads the GDT, but this time using the highmem location, and sets up a stack after the archive. The size is extracted from the Multiboot header. Knowing the start address, the C code can then iterate over itself to locate and access files in the archive.
Some linker script trickery is used to tie it all into one blob, but with the GDT and Multiboot header visible from both lomem and highmem code at different locations.
At this point, you might be inclined to actually read the source code in the ZIP archive. There are lots of comments trying to explain what is going on.
There's a README that points out the structure of the code with suggestions where to start reading. I decided to keep it readable rather than stuff it all into a single sector. Self-modifying trickery is kept to a minimum (to safe some space, the function to enter unreal mode modifies itself, the code is run twice, courtesy of a misdirected ret, entering protected mode the first time round, leaving it again and restoring the segment registers on the second run, before returning for real).
Code in the archive and this blog posts have been written with assistance from:
If you poke around in the code and have any suggestions for improvements, or otherwise do anything interesting with it, please let me know.
Have fun!

articles.title: Amazon Expands Drone Deliveries, and Gets Noise Complaints. 'Like a Swarm of Bees'
articles.body:
Amazon Expands Drone Deliveries, and Gets Noise Complaints. 'Like a Swarm of Bees' (chron.com) 28
			
		 	
				"In August, Amazon announced it was expanding its airborne shipping to suburban areas in nearly 500 U.S. cities," reports the Chicago Sun-Times, "including the Chicago, Atlanta, Cleveland and Boise, Idaho, metro areas."  And on Tuesday Amazon cut the ribbon on its new drone delivery center Tuesday 24 miles south of Chicago.
But Amazon's drones are already servicing parts of Texas, notes the Houston Chronicle.  And  north of Houston, Theresa Gibbons complains "It was kind of cool and fascinating at first, but now it is driving me crazy."
Her home in the Bridgestone neighborhood is nestled right in the flight path of Amazon's drone service. Gibson said she hears roughly a dozen drones flying over her home each day.   Noise pollution has become a frequent complaint in Texas neighborhoods where the service operates. Residents have compared the sound to everything from a massive beehive to a full-on air raid. "It does not sound like a [single] bumble bee. It sounds like a large swarm of bees at a much higher volume than a normal swarm of bees. And it's all day long," said Gibson.
Amazon's drone delivery service is currently operating in four Texas cities, including Houston, Waco, San Antonio and Richardson. The company announced major expansion plans in August, but growing complaints in pilot neighborhoods could foreshadow complications later down the line, with regions such as Harris County already taking legal action in response... So far, a group of fifteen states, plus Harris County,  [Texas] have formed a coalition that has filed a petition in the US Court of Appeals challenging the Federal Aviation Administration's environmental review, citing that it failed to adequately address the effects of expanding drone deliveries.    
And meanwhile near Boise, Idaho, local news station KTVB reports....
Less than two weeks after Amazon began delivering packages by drone in Nampa, the cities of Nampa and Meridian say they have received complaints over the noise and how often the drones fly...  Amazon began Prime Air drone deliveries Oct. 30 from its East Franklin Road fulfillment center, making Nampa the company's first Idaho drone site... 
How people feel about the drones depends on whom you ask. A Meridian man who has received drone deliveries says the noise doesn't bother him. Neighbors closest to the launch site say the drones fly from sunup to sundown and are disturbing their peace.  Randy Nye, who has lived in Cherry Creek Estates for 17 years, compared it to living in a beehive.  "It's just a constant presence," he said....  Nye, who works from home, said he and his neighbors who technically are just outside city limits had no idea this was coming. He said the city approved the drones in May, and they were never given written notice this was coming, despite living so close. He said they were shocked when deliveries started by drones just 12 days ago.  Nye said he hopes something can change. 
A few homes down, Kerri Wattier has started counting. On Wednesday with KTVB, she clicked a handheld counter each time a drone passed over her home. She started at 3:30 p.m. By 4:18 p.m., she had counted 39.  "It sounds like lawnmowers and leaf blowers flying over our house," Wattier said.  
"Amazon says it is evaluating changes, including adjusting flight paths," the article adds.
Ironically at that ribbon-cutting ceremony near Chicago, the speakers were occasionally drowned out by the roar of the drones, reports the Chicago Tribune, since they're "relatively loud when they are close to the ground."  ("At the point of delivery they top out at 68 decibels," said Amazon economic development manager Sam Bailey, adding that "It's very brief exposure and it only occurs during daytime hours.")
But that site has been operational since October 12, and has "generally" hit its maximum capacity of 300 drone orders daily, Bailey told the Chicago Tribune, adding that scaling up is "something that we're always considering."  And since October 12 they've already seen "thousands" of orders delivered by their 21 drones just across that 7.5-mile radius:
Bailey said customers should clear the area when a drone delivery is incoming. The drones drop packages from about 12 feet. If the drone detects movement in the area, he said, the delivery will be canceled.  "You want your kids inside the house," Bailey said. "We will not drop a package in an unsafe location. People who want to stand below and try to catch it, don't do that." 
The Chicago Sun-Times points out that Walmart already offers some drone deliveries from over 75 stores across Arkansas, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia and Texas, and "earlier this year said it planned to expand drone delivery service to 150 more stores in partnership with Wing, a division of Google parent company Alphabet, giving it 270 drone delivery locations by 2027."

articles.title: US IRS free online tax filing open source repo (2025)
articles.body:
Direct File is a service from the United States Government that provides taxpayers the option to electronically file their federal tax return for free, directly with the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Direct File is an interview-based service that is intended to work as well on a mobile phone as it does on a laptop, tablet, or desktop computer. It is available in English and Spanish and is designed to be accessible to taxpayers who have a variety of attitudes, aptitudes, abilities, and access needs.
Direct File interprets the United States' Internal Revenue Code (26 USC) as plain language questions, the answers to which should be known to taxpayers without need of external instructions or publications. Taxpayers' answers are then translated into standard tax forms and transmitted to the IRS's Modernized e-File (MeF) API, which is available for authorized public use. These questions and logic, developed in close collaboration with the IRS Office of Chief Counsel, as well as the associated test cases and scenarios, may be useful for others working on products that need to accurately interpret United States tax law as of Tax Year 2024.
Direct File also incorporates the Fact Graph, a declarative, XML-based knowledge graph data structure that is designed to reason about incomplete information, such as a partially completed tax return. The Fact Graph is written in the Scala programming language; it runs on the JVM on the backend and is transpiled via Scala.js to run on the client as well. Direct File's Fact Graph is not domain-specific, and it may be useful to revenue agencies and as a reference for business rules engine implementations.
Although Direct File only files federal tax returns, United States taxpayers also have state and local filing obligations. Direct File facilitates the completion of these obligations by enabling taxpayers to optionally import their federal return data into a third-party tool that can file state and/or local taxes, without needing to reenter information. This transaction is enabled via a State API, which transfers both standard MeF XML as well as an enriched JSON format that includes additional data elements that were identified as being useful to state revenue agencies to streamline the state tax experience.
Direct File was developed by an in-house team of technologists at the IRS. The blended, cross-agency team included support from USDS and GSA, as well as vendor teams TrussWorks, Coforma, and ATI.
For a more details on the program and its history see https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p5969.pdf and https://www.irs.gov/filing/irs-direct-file-for-free
This repository has been archived and is no longer maintained. The code is provided for historical reference and may contain unpatched or unknown vulnerabilities. It should not be used in production systems.
See ONBOARDING.md if you want to jump into running Direct File locally
Not all source code, documentation and metadata used in the development of Direct File is included in this repository. Specifically, any code or data that is considered Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Federal Tax Information (FTI), Sensitive But Unclassified (SBU), or source code developed for National Security Systems (NSS), as defined in 40 U.S.C. § 11103, is exempt. Due to these restrictions, certain pieces of functionality have been removed or rewritten.
Legal foundations for work include:
- Source code Harmonization And Reuse in Information Technology Act" of 2024, Public Law 118 - 187
- OMB Memorandum M-16-21, “Federal Source Code Policy: Achieving Efficiency, Transparency, and Innovation through Reusable and Open Source Software,” August 8, 2016
- Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Part 27 – Patents, Data, and Copyrights
- Digital Government Strategy: “Digital Government: Building a 21st Century Platform to Better Serve the American People,” May 23, 2012
- Federal Information Technology Acquisition Reform Act (FITARA), December 2014 (National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2015, Title VIII, Subtitle D)
- E-Government Act of 2002, Public Law 107-347
- Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, Public Law 104-106

articles.title: 50th Anniversary of 'Star Wars' Celebrated with iMax 70mm Re-Release, Special Events, New Movie
articles.body:
50th Anniversary of 'Star Wars' Celebrated with iMax 70mm Re-Release, Special Events, New Movie (deadline.com) 35
			
		 	
				"Lucasfilm and Disney have restored the original Star Wars (1977) and will release the film in multiple formats, including Imax 70mm [starting February 19], as part of the franchise's 50th anniversary celebrations," reports Deadline.
The original film will also be displayed in its original 16:9 format on the center of Cosm's 12K+ LED Dome, in a special presentation developed with Disney, Lucasfilm, ILM, and MakeMake.  They're calling it a "Shared Reality production" where "the surrounding visual environments dynamically evolve to immerse the audience in iconic Star Wars locations and moments."
Deadline reports more 50th anniversary celebrations
In addition to the Imax 70mm screenings, the film will also be presented in Digital Imax, Digital Cinema, 70mm, 35mm, and 4DX.    On May 4th, 2027, Lucasfilm will release a new behind-the-scenes documentary, The Hero Awakens, from filmmaker R.J. Cutler on Disney+.   Star Wars events already on the calendar for 2027 include Shawn Levy's [movie]  Star Wars: Starfighter, which will be released May 28. 
There's also a new poster paying homage to the original 1977 film, reports the Disney news site Mickey Visit, plus a newly orchestrated score by John Williams that they assume "will be used on all the projects that debut this year."
On April 2-3, [Disney] will debut the new "Star Wars in Concert: The Skywalker Saga" at the Hollywood Bowl. The show will be hosted by Anthony Daniels, known for his role as C-3PO.  Special performances of John Williams' iconic film scores will feature scenes and music from all nine Skywalker Saga films. The concert is a sweeping celebration of the stories, themes, and music that have inspired audiences around the world for five decades...
They also teased that new and legacy licensees — including Hasbro, the LEGO Group, adidas, Mars, Aston Martin, Steinway, Hajime Sorayama presented by Complex, and more — will introduce 50th-anniversary collections... In the opening of the press release, Disney mentioned that as part of the announcements there will be "reimagined Disney Parks and Cruise Line offerings."
  
The article adds that the April's Star Wars Celebration at the Los Angeles Convention Center has already sold out.
There's more Star Wars news, writes long-time Slashdot reader schwit1
A light saber used by Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" movies The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi sold Thursday for nearly $5 million in an auction.   The light saber, which was used in the climactic duel in Cloud City in which Vader tells Luke Skywalker "I am your father" sold for $4.875 million at the Ultimate Star Wars Auction held by Heritage Auctions. The sale marks a world auction record for any "Star Wars" collectible, according to the auction house. 
The previous record was Heritage's $3,750,000 sale of Luke Skywalker's lightsaber and severed hand effects rig on July 15, 2026.  And they're still auctioning more Star Wars memorabilia...

articles.title: Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
articles.body:
A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.
The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.
The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.
“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.
Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs.
Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding.

articles.title: The MacBook Pro's OLED PWM Problem: When a 'Better' Display Becomes Worse to Use
articles.body:
The MacBook Pro’s OLED PWM Problem: When a ‘Better’ Display Becomes Worse to Use
Apple has made a spectacular display. But spectacular isn’t the same as comfortable, and the people discovering that distinction deserve to be heard.
Apple has brought tandem OLED technology to the MacBook Pro, joining the Mini-LED display that has served the range since 2021 (and which Apple continues to sell). Apple calls this a “PROLED XDR Display”. It features individually illuminated pixels, effectively infinite contrast, wonderfully deep blacks and the sort of image quality that Mini-LED, for all its considerable strengths, can’t fully equal. Peak HDR brightness has increased, and Apple has introduced a new display engine designed to manage colour, luminance and pixel usage with extraordinary precision. And of course, in a first for any Apple notebook display, it has touch-input capability.
When Apple unveiled the new MacBook Pro, the initial reaction to the screen was overwhelmingly positive.
But there’s a burgeoning discussion taking place within the Mac community that deserves attention. On MacRumors forums, a thread titled RIP MacBook Pro PROLED for PWM Sensitive Eyes - apple cmon! has attracted people describing remarkably similar experiences. Discussions are also appearing across Reddit, with owners describing discomfort shortly after using their new machines. Some report headaches; others describe a strange sensation of eye fatigue, dizziness, nausea, or an inability to concentrate on the screen for extended periods. Some have already returned the device.
Mike Wuerthele, of AppleInsider, published an article on 10 November titled If you’re getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone, examining these reports.
The following caveat probably doesn't need to be made, but I will make it anyway: these are individual experiences, not evidence that the new MacBook Pro is causing problems for everyone. Plenty of owners are likely perfectly content with (and dazzled by) their new displays. But that isn’t really the point. For the people experiencing these symptoms, the fact that somebody else can happily spend several hours staring at the same screen isn’t particularly reassuring, especially given Apple's long-standing commitment to accessibility. A display can be technically spectacular and still be a spectacularly poor display for a subset of people.
PWM
Much of the discussion centres on Pulse Width Modulation, or PWM. It’s a technique used to control screen brightness by rapidly switching or modulating the light output. On an OLED display, the pixels themselves produce the light, rather than relying on a separate backlight. By varying the way that light output is modulated, the display can control its apparent brightness.
At sufficiently high frequencies, this flickering isn’t something most people can consciously detect. But some people are particularly sensitive to this kind of modulation and can experience eye strain, headaches and other forms of discomfort when looking at displays that use it.
This is a pretty good demonstration of PWM on an M4 iPad Pro, which also has a tandem OLED display:
Neither PWM nor the discussion surrounding it is new. It’s been a talking point for years, particularly around OLED displays, and something manufacturers have increasingly had to consider as display technology has evolved (including Apple — more on this later).
Notebookcheck, which conducted laboratory testing of the 14-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, measured PWM at 240Hz. This is its worst-case reading, with flickering detected at brightness settings of 99% and below.
To put that into perspective, the M4 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED display measured 14,880Hz in Notebookcheck’s testing. At 240Hz, the brightness fluctuation repeats 240 times per second; at 14,880Hz, it repeats almost 15,000 times per second. That’s one hell of a difference. The reported modulation frequency of the new MacBook Pro’s OLED panel is roughly 62 times lower than that measured on the Mini-LED model.[1]
Frequency isn’t the only consideration, though. The extent to which brightness fluctuates during each cycle also matters, as do the characteristics of the display’s dimming system. We shouldn’t assume that these figures translate directly into how comfortable somebody will find a particular display. There’s no simple, one-size-fits-all formula for predicting who will experience problems.
It’s also worth avoiding the temptation to treat PWM as a universal explanation for every headache or instance of eye strain. Screen discomfort can have numerous causes. Some users’ discomfort may have nothing to do with PWM.[2]
Wait, isn’t OLED supposed to be better?
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is emphatically not an inexpensive laptop with a budget screen. This is Apple’s flagship professional notebook. The PROLED XDR configuration represents a substantial investment, and the display is arguably its most important selling point. Apple has spent years refining its displays, and there’s a reasonable expectation that moving to OLED should represent some sort of improvement in almost every meaningful respect, especially given the savagely high price tag of these new machines.

The new MacBook Pro appears to use a combination of PWM and DC dimming. Notebookcheck notes that DC dimming is present across brightness levels, but that the panel still exhibits 240Hz flickering.

One of the problems with PWM discussions is that they tend to quickly become highly polarised. Someone says they experience headaches, and someone else responds that they’ve been using OLED displays for years without any issues. Two things can be true at once.

This matters because PWM sensitivity is often discussed as though it’s a straightforward, binary distinction between people who can tolerate OLED and people who can’t. But as soon as I look at the screen for more than a minute, the dizziness comes back.
This is first machine in 20 years as an Apple customer that I return literally anything. Too bad, because the laptop is amazing in all aspects otherwise, I was in love with it the moment I took it out of the box (coming from an M1 Pro 16 inch). It would have been my daily driver for the next 5 years. So, now I am waiting for the M7 variant and hope they will find a way to mitigate this issue. I am returning the MacBook tomorrow morning after less than a week of using it.
Apple has built up a loyal audience of professional Mac users who spend enormous amounts of money on the machines, and enormous amounts of time in front of their displays. Photographers, designers, developers, writers and video editors can spend entire working days looking at a MacBook screen (I do). So imagine upgrading from an M4 or M5 Pro MacBook Pro with Mini-LED, expecting a more beautiful version of something you already love, only to discover that you can’t comfortably use the new machine for more than a short period. Good customer experience is usually Apple's guiding North Star. Bad customer experience is usually Apple’s Kryptonite.
Has Apple compromised on the wrong thing?
There are plenty of engineering considerations involved in developing a tandem OLED panel for a laptop — brightness, power consumption, thermal management, longevity, colour accuracy and uniformity all have to be balanced.
Apple's displays have always involved trade-offs to one degree or another. Take the Mini-LED display — while it's truly excellent in many respects, it notoriously suffers from blooming (an inherent limitation of Mini-LED local dimming) and has also typically had poor pixel response times. These are compromises Apple has had to accept in order to deliver the particular combination of brightness, contrast and HDR performance that makes the Mini-LED display so impressive.
Apple has made some ambitious claims about the new PROLED XDR display, particularly around its brightness and the intelligence of its display engine. We don’t know why Apple has ended up with this particular dimming behaviour, or what trade-offs were involved in achieving it. But I think it’s reasonable to ask whether display comfort received enough consideration in the process. The new MacBook Pro produces extraordinary blacks, stunning HDR highlights and exceptionally accurate colours, and so on. But none of that matters particularly much if the person sitting in front of it develops a headache, or feels like they want to throw up when they're using it.
When the majority experience isn’t everyone’s experience
People experiencing unusual, poorly understood or relatively uncommon health problems have often found themselves struggling to be heard — they have to explain their symptoms repeatedly, defend their experiences and convince others that their difficulties are genuine. I don't personally know anybody who suffers from PWM sensitivity, and I appreciate that it can be difficult for someone without these experiences to understand how something so ordinary could become a source of physical discomfort for another person. But personal experience shouldn't be a prerequisite for compassion. We don’t need to experience somebody else’s symptoms to acknowledge that they are struggling.
Stories like this tend to surface only once an ill-defined and arbitrary threshold of people complaining is crossed. But even if something only affects a small minority, doesn’t that minority matter? Apple certainly appears to care about the minority — they put an extraordinary amount of work into accessibility features, many of which are incredibly important to relatively small groups of users. It’s one of the things which sets Apple apart. Features such as VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch and other accessibility technologies exist because Apple recognises that different people interact with technology in different ways. Why shouldn’t display comfort receive similar consideration? It doesn’t mean Apple must abandon OLED, or compromise the experience for everyone. It means offering alternatives where technically feasible.
Apple previously introduced a ‘Display Pulse Smoothing option’ on supported iPhone models. It’s an accessibility setting which can be toggled in the Settings app. Apple describes Display Pulse Smoothing as a way to create a smoother dimming experience at low brightness on supported iPhones. Its support documentation cautions that disabling PWM may affect low-brightness display performance under certain conditions. It took Apple a long time to include this feature by the way (it arrived nearly 8 years after the iPhone X was released). Incidentally, Apple has also included Display Pulse Smoothing on the new iPad mini with OLED display.
Could something similar be offered on the Mac? We shouldn’t assume that a software feature would completely resolve the issue. Changing the way the display is driven could introduce other compromises, and Apple would need to implement it carefully. But even a degree of user control would be gratefully received.
For now, anyone concerned about PWM sensitivity should be cautious about buying the new machine without trying it first. A quick demo in an Apple Store isn’t necessarily representative of spending an entire working day in front of the display. Don’t assume that being comfortable with an OLED iPhone means you’ll be comfortable with this MacBook. If you experience discomfort, don’t assume that increasing brightness or changing colour settings will necessarily resolve it.
The existing Mini-LED MacBook Pro thankfully remains a viable alternative for people who have found that display comfortable. But the Mini-LED MacBook Pro might not stay around for much longer. Apple looks to be transitioning to OLED across their devices — this may have consequences unless Apple changes the way they're implementing this particular technology.
The best MacBook display isn’t necessarily the best display for everyone
We sometimes get so caught up in the pursuit of better specifications that we forget what these devices are actually for. The most important part of a display is that it's something you sit in front of for hours at a time.
Displays to my mind are like mattresses — they're not something you should compromise on, unless financial constraints demand it. I've often been puzzled why people baulk at paying a lot for a display when they’re likely going to be using it for several hours a day. Similarly, I’ve often wondered why people baulk at paying a lot of money for a mattress, when they’re going to be spending roughly a third of their lives lying on one. A decent mattress is probably something you should invest in. The specs of the mattress matter, of course, and individual comfort matters enormously. The same thing is true with a display, which is why I have no issue having spent the money I did on a Studio Display XDR.
And this is what's so problematic with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display. According to many reviewers this is one of the best displays they've ever seen, and it has a price to match. Starting at £2899 for the 14-inch version (£3399 for the 16-inch), boy is it expensive. If the technology responsible for making the PROLED XDR Display look spectacular also makes it uncomfortable for some people to use, then we need to ask if that trade-off is worth it.
I suspect most people buying the new MacBook Pro will never think about PWM. They’ll open the lid, admire the display and get on with their lives. But for the people who have discovered that they can no longer comfortably use the latest MacBook Pro, this is a really big deal.
I’d like to see Apple explain why the new display behaves so differently from the Mini-LED panel used in other MacBook Pro models, and whether there’s any possibility of improving its dimming characteristics through software. Perhaps there’s a perfectly reasonable engineering explanation. Perhaps there are limitations inherent in this particular panel.
I’d be interested to hear from anyone who has experienced this first-hand, particularly those who have previously used Apple’s OLED iPhones or iPads without difficulty, but are now struggling with the new MacBook Pro.
Get in touch at hello@macanorak.com
You can also submit feedback to Apple here: https://www.apple.com/feedback/macbook-pro/
- A 62-fold difference in frequency doesn’t translate into a 62-fold difference in comfort. It doesn’t work that way. Frequency, modulation depth and individual sensitivity all matter. ↩︎
- It may have to do with what type of screen they’ve opted for — glossy, or nano-texture. A personal example here: I have the nano-texture screen on the MacBook Pro, my iPad Pro and my iPhone Duo, and I get along with those just fine. But I could not get along with nano-texture on Apple's range of Studio Displays — it caused me a lot of visual discomfort / headaches — moving to glossy screens with those monitors has treated me much better in that regard. ↩︎
